articles.title: Automating Reproducibility Checks Using Large Language Models
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Computational reproducibility checks are essential to scientific credibility, yet few published papers are ever independently verified, largely because manual checking is labor-intensive and time-consuming. We tested whether an agentic large language model (LLM) could perform computational reproducibility checks at scale. We benchmarked computational reproducibility checks performed by an LLM analyst (Claude Opus running in the Claude Code harness) against results from expert-led reproducibility audits in the social and behavioral sciences and found that LLM accuracy was comparable to that of human experts. Agentic LLMs can now perform high-quality reproducibility checks relatively cheaply, quickly, and easily, putting large-scale audits within reach for journals, granting agencies, organizations, and individual researchers.

articles.title: Why don’t web survey panelists complete a survey? An analysis of response refusal and discontinuation
articles.authors: Tai Kurosawa
articles.abstract: Not all participants complete web surveys distributed by web research companies. Some refuse to participate in the survey, whereas others discontinue their responses. This study examined the extent of similarity in the reasons for refusal and discontinuation among research company panelists, as well as the associations between refusal and discontinuation and demographic information and sense of busyness. In Study 1, data from 500 participants from a research company were analyzed. In Study 2, data from 600 participants from a research company were analyzed. The results showed that a large number of surveys being distributed was associated with a higher response rate, and the importance of the factors of refusal and discontinuation varied across groups. The findings are discussed with reference to the leverage-salience theory.

articles.title: A decision support toolkit for AI-ready neuroscience data governance
articles.authors: Wilhelmina M. Botes; Artur Mendes; Bart Huffman; Madison Fleischaker; Ciara Staunton; Beverley Townsend; Paul Ogendi; Lukman Abdulrauf; Andrea Parziale; Gabriela Skoczylas-Kizak
articles.abstract:
Contemporary human neuroscience relies on exchanging and analyzing neurodata across global institutions and
jurisdictions. However, regulatory architecture fails to maintain continuity of protection across distributed research
environments. Our comparison of 93 countries and 10 operative governance units across Africa, Europe, Latin
America and the Caribbean, and North America shows that neurodata are rarely recognized as distinct regulatory
objects, usually falling under broader legal classifications. While international sharing is permitted in principle,
transformation into derivatives, embeddings, and AI models raises questions about the scope and implementation of
continuing safeguards. We show that international exchange is defined by conditional interoperability, where effective
safeguards require aligning legal, institutional, and technical controls. To operationalize these findings, we introduce a
modular governance toolkit for the data-to-model lifecycle, including a Neurodata Risk Classification Framework,
decision support tools for neurodata transfer and transformation, and a Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement to
sustain protection without global legal harmonization.

articles.title: Audience engagement in live and recorded performance: a social liveness perspective
articles.authors: Robin Ren; Joseph Devlin; John S Hogan; Jorina von Zimmermann; Helen Nuttall; Daniel C. Richardson
articles.abstract: The best memories in life are often collective, from the roar of a stadium to the applause in a concert hall. The value of those moments can be seen in ratings of engagement, feelings of social affiliation, and synchronies in behaviour and autonomic arousal. But what exactly produces the value of the collective experience of a performance? Is it the presence of performers (physical liveness), the presence of other audience members (social liveness), or the fact they are sharing a stimulus? We looked at a range of collective experiences from live theatre to public cinemas to small group viewing in which we varied the two dimensions of liveness and tracked engagement through physiological synchrony. Our goal was to explore some of the many elements that contribute to liveness and engagement. We found that higher liveness, whether physical or social, fostered higher audience engagement and elevated heart rate synchrony. However, co-present pairs were not always more synchronised than pseudo-pairs who watched the same narrative stimuli at different times, suggesting that collective entrainment is not a uniform consequence of ‘being together’. We argue that while many dimensions of sociality might contribute to social liveness, understanding how they combine, how they are balanced with the narrative stimuli to foster collective entrainment without being distracted is the key to creating an engaging collective experience.

articles.title: Can Chimpanzees Imagine a Blue Banana?
articles.authors: Andrey Vyshedskiy
articles.abstract: Can a chimpanzee that has learned words for colors and objects find a blue pencil among pencils, straws, and Lego pieces in red, green, and blue? This seemingly simple task requires more than recognizing individual words: it requires integrating the meaning of a color adjective with that of a noun to identify an object possessing both properties. Children typically master this ability by 2.3 years. By age 3, they can integrate two modifiers, such as size and color, to follow instructions like “Find a large green straw.” These achievements mark important milestones in the development of language comprehension, allowing children to combine multiple words into a unified mental representation of an object. Chimpanzees, by contrast, can learn hundreds of words referring to objects, colors, and actions. Yet, despite decades of research, they have not been demonstrated to reliably integrate even a color with a noun. In this paper, we propose a simple neurocognitive account of adjective–noun comprehension. We argue that this ability depends on the development of neural connections that allow the prefrontal cortex to modify sensory representations of objects in posterior cortical regions. This framework offers a testable explanation for a fundamental difference between human and chimpanzee language comprehension.

articles.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
articles.authors: Pablo Arias Sarah; Guillaume Denis; Philippe schyns; Rachael Jack; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall; Jean-Julien Aucouturier
articles.abstract:
Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researchers
cannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recent
advances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental control
over the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientific
videoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,
realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record the
synchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In a
preregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fully
online setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remaining
undetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocal
and verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimental
control and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causal
experimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.

articles.title: Speaking through shared hubs, not gendered spokes? Exploring sex-related variation in object naming in Tunisian Arabic-speaking people with post-stroke aphasia
articles.authors: Amina KLIBI
articles.abstract: Whether sex-related factors shape confrontational object naming in non-Western clinical populations remains understudied within the Controlled Semantic Cognition framework. We evaluated naming performance across eight semantic categories and three overall measures in 14 native Tunisian Arabic speakers with post-stroke aphasia (6 males, 8 females). Group differences were examined using nonparametric Mann–Whitney U tests and Bayesian analyses. Uncorrected comparisons initially favored female patients in Furniture naming (p = .023) and Total Immediate Responses (p = .043). However, no category-level differences survived correction for multiple comparisons. Bayesian analyses predominantly supported the null hypothesis (BF₀₁ = 1.24–2.15), with Furniture showing only weak, inconclusive evidence for a sex effect (BF₁₀ = 1.93). Overall, results provide no convincing evidence of systematic sex-related disparities in object naming. These findings align with a shared amodal semantic hub rather than gendered spokes, though larger studies are required to confirm sex invariance in this population.

articles.title: The Unappreciated Helper: When an AI Facilitation Agent Improves Group Efficiency Despite Poorer User Perceptions
articles.authors: Nicolas Michinov; Marinette Bouet; Eric Jamet; Axel Mascaro; Muriel Noël; Albane Pechard; Farouk Toumani; Zineddine Zahouani; Estelle Michinov
articles.abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence make it possible to embed AI facilitation agents in collaborative settings, where they can deliver real-time recommendations based on ongoing group discussions. This experimental study examined how group members perceive a collaborative platform with or without such an agent and evaluated the agent’s effects on group communication and performance. A total of 187 undergraduate psychology students collaborated in 50 groups of three or four members on a digital platform with a synchronous text chat. Groups were randomly assigned to one of two conditions (25 groups per condition): with an AI facilitation agent (n = 96 participants) that encouraged information sharing when exchanges were insufficient, or without the agent (n = 91 participants). Participants rated the platform’s acceptability, perceived support, sense of intrusion, and affective reactions. Participants in the AI condition rated the platform as less acceptable and less supportive, but not more intrusive or unpleasant. Nevertheless, groups assisted by the agent were more efficient, completing the task faster with less communicative effort. Descriptive analyses of group interactions in the three minutes before and after the agent’s interventions showed a shift from providing information toward requesting information, expressing opinions, and agreeing, without change in overall interaction volume. These findings reveal a gap between objective performance and subjective perceptions, highlighting the need to design AI agents that improve group efficiency while fostering members’ sense of support and acceptance.

articles.title: Who Will Conduct Science?  Researchers’ Expectations of AI Capabilities and the Future of Scientific Work
articles.authors: Balazs Aczel; Dianovics Dominik; Peter Szecsi; Barnabas Szaszi
articles.abstract: Recent advances in generative AI systems have demonstrated their potential to outperform humans in conducting research and in answering previously unsolved scientific problems. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing research independently, the question shifts from how researchers should use AI to how much human resources will be required in scientific research and where. We surveyed researchers worldwide about their perspectives on AI-driven scientific research, prompted by OpenAI’s bulk release of mathematical solutions in October 2026. We received over 4,000 responses from researchers across 126 countries and a wide range of disciplines. Most respondents (62%) expected AI systems to be capable of conducting research tasks independently within three years, although expectations regarding the quality of AI-generated research varied, with 41% anticipating quality comparable to or exceeding that of competent human researchers. Respondents generally supported allowing AI to assume most roles in scientific research (each with a minimum of 48%), mainly under human supervision. AI developments made one-third of respondents concerned about their own job security; mathematicians and statisticians anticipated the greatest effects on their research and careers (45%), and researchers in the humanities and arts the least (30%). Despite concerns about potential negative career consequences, respondents overwhelmingly (74%) expected AI-driven research to accelerate scientific progress. Although the limitations of this survey restrict the generalizability of its findings, the results offer an overview of how researchers across more than a hundred countries perceive rapid advances in AI. They also highlight the need to monitor AI’s impact on the scientific workforce and inform policies that support the sustainable integration of AI into scientific research.

articles.title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Federica Moro; Gianmatteo Farabolini
articles.abstract: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.

articles.title: Psychological essentialism, compression and the structure of concepts
articles.authors: Peter Gärdenfors; Matias Osta-Vélez
articles.abstract:
Psychological essentialism is the tendency to view the members of categories as sharing a
hidden essence that explains their observable properties. From a cognitive point of view,
essentialist beliefs depend partly on judgments that several properties of objects ‘hang
together.
’ As a consequence, humans perceive natural kind categories as having stronger
essences than other categories, such as artifact categories. In this paper, we offer a new way to
explain essentialism as the result of a process of dimensionality reduction involved in the
formation of concepts. More specifically, we propose that a small set of principal components
(as understood from Principal Component Analysis) represents patterns of covariation that can
support essentialist beliefs about categories. We show that our approach accounts for several
empirical findings concerning psychological essentialism. We also discuss how to understand
the functional properties in artifact categories, and the connection between generic language
and essentialism from a developmental perspective.

articles.title: Dan Parker, Linguistic illusions: A case study on agreement attraction. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2025. Pp. xvi + 171.
articles.authors: Radim Lacina; Utku Turk
articles.abstract: This is a review of Dan Parker's book 'Linguistic illusions: A case study on agreement attraction' published by Cambridge University Press in 2025. The book gives a comprehensive summary of both the basics of a myriad of illusory phenomena and of agreement attraction in detail. It is a valuable resource for students and researchers alike, especially thanks to the accessible explanations of the leading issues and theories in the field. We critically discuss the book's reported ACT-R modelling, original experiments and its limited engagement with the cross-linguistic study of attraction.

articles.title: Depressive symptoms are associated with weaker evidence accumulation and greater caution during social decision-making
articles.authors: Jinil Kim; Yuan-Wei Yao
articles.abstract: Depression is often characterized by reduced reward sensitivity, slowed responding, and altered social functioning. Prior drift-diffusion modeling studies have linked depression to less efficient accumulation of decision evidence and to greater decision caution in non-social decision-making tasks. However, it remains unclear whether similar process-level alterations extend to social decision-making tasks, such as the ultimatum game, which involves weighing monetary reward against emotional reactions to another player’s offer. To address this question, we applied drift-diffusion models to a publicly available dataset in which 351 adults, grouped by the Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D), responded to offers in the ultimatum game. Participants with elevated depressive symptoms accepted offers at a rate comparable to those with lower symptoms but responded more slowly. In a standard time-stationary diffusion model, the high depressive-symptom group showed weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, indexed by lower drift rate and wider decision thresholds, respectively. In an exploratory time-varying model that allowed different attributes to enter the decision process at different times, the same group differences in drift rate and decision threshold were observed. Additionally, the difference between reward and emotion information was estimated to enter the decision process later in the high depressive-symptom group. These findings suggest that depression-related slowing during social decision-making may arise from weaker evidence accumulation and greater decision caution, which are not apparent from acceptance rates alone.

articles.title: Stereotypes of Epistemic Sources and Conspiracy Beliefs: The Primacy of Perceived Morality
articles.authors: Deniz Bayramoğlu; Sinan Alper
articles.abstract: The present study examines how stereotypes of epistemic sources predict conspiracy beliefs through the lens of the Stereotype Content Model (SCM). Two studies with nationally representative samples from the United Kingdom (N = 290) and the United States (N = 289) assessed perceptions of doctors, academics, journalists, and government officials in terms of sociability, morality, competence, and assertiveness, alongside general and profession-specific conspiracy beliefs. Correlational and random forest regression analyses showed that perceived morality was the most consistent and robust predictor across professions, with lower perceived morality associated with higher conspiracy beliefs. Other dimensions showed more context-dependent associations: Competence occasionally contributed, particularly for academics; sociability varied across professions; and assertiveness was generally a weak predictor. These findings suggest that conspiracy beliefs regarding epistemic authorities are more consistently associated with perceived moral character than with perceived expertise, although competence also played a role, particularly for academics.

articles.title: Do Scales Semantically Resemble the Sources They Cite? Embedding Analysis of Construct Proliferation in Five Anomy Instruments
articles.authors: Mateo Belalcazar; Joan Sebastian Diaz Mona; Nelson Molina Valencia; Yenny Otálora
articles.abstract:
Construct proliferation in psychology is associated with jingle and jangle fallacies that psychometric methods are not designed to detect. Semantic embeddings offer a complementary approach, but existing applications have compared scales within a single level without bringing in the theoretical texts a construct's tradition rests on. This study extends the embedding framework of Wulff and Mata (2025a) to a
cross-level comparison paired with a documentary audit of citation acts. We embedded 43 items from five anomy scales alongside 3,762 propositions extracted from nine source texts at three analytical levels (foundational texts, scale articles, and items), using six embedding models from three architectural families, and we coded every passage in which a scale article cites a theoretical source. Items formed
  thematic clusters that crossed scale boundaries, beyond the expression of a single homogeneous theme per instrument, while retaining within-scale cohesion, and were rarely nearest to the article that introduced them (14%). All five scale articles were semantically nearest to Merton's (1938) text, a pattern identical across models, stable under bootstrap resampling, and not reproduced by two genre-matched control texts. The documentary audit showed that no article adopts Merton's formulation; the two articles that adopt a foundational text both adopt Durkheim's Suicide, which was the nearest foundation for neither of them. This proximity coexists with the absence of any direct adoption of Merton. This extension, combining semantic proximity with documented citation acts, offers an approach for examining whether the sources an instrument cites are also the ones its content most resembles.

articles.title: The Political is Relational: Political Dissimilarity Predicts Worse Relationship Quality and Likelihood of Breakup
articles.authors: Yitong Zhao; Stephanie Domingo; Noah M. Laskey; Matthew Feinberg; Spike W. S. Lee; Brett Quaid Ford
articles.abstract: Politics is not just about policy—it can become deeply personal, straining relationships between family members, friends, and romantic partners who hold different political views. Extending prior work that mostly focused on romantic relationships in non-representative samples, we tested whether political dissimilarity predicted worse relationship quality across romantic and non-romantic close relationships in a nationally representative U.S. sample (N = 1,075; 45% Republican, 55% Democrat) during a period of heightened political tension around the 2024 U.S. election. In a ten-wave longitudinal study spanning September 2024 to October 2025, greater political dissimilarity predicted worse relationship quality and a 22% higher odds of relationship breakup. These effects were comparable across various sociodemographics and close relationship types, indicating broad generalizability. These findings underscore the widespread relational costs of political dissimilarity: Political divides spill deeply into personal life, eroding the quality and stability of people’s closest ties.

articles.title: Neural Correlates of Partner Comparisons and Their Links to Intimate Partner Aggression
articles.authors: Sydney Kavanaugh; Alexandra Martelli; Samuel James West; Emily Lasko; David Skylan Chester
articles.abstract: People frequently compare themselves to their intimate partners. These partner comparisons are critical for relationship maintenance, with powerful ramifications for intimate partner aggression (IPA) perpetration. However, little is known about the neural correlates of partner comparisons and their relation to IPA perpetration. To address this gap, 96 participants from 49 intimate partner dyads underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and completed a social comparison task, judging their own negative and positive traits against those of their partner and the average person. Participants then reported whether they had any history of IPA perpetration. Consistent with previous findings, participants reported having less negative and more positive traits than others. However, participants’ tendency to compare themselves favorably to others was attenuated for their partners. Partner (> average person) comparisons were linked to heightened activity in the mentalizing network (DMPFC, precuneus, TPJ) and DLPFC, particularly for negative traits. Such DLPFC/DMPFC activity during partner comparisons related to greater IPA perpetration for negative traits and lesser IPA perpetration for positive traits. These findings suggest that recruiting mentalizing and executive control networks during partner comparisons may be meaningfully linked to IPA perpetration, depending on trait valence.

articles.title: Regulating Self-Interest: The Effect of Anodal tDCS over the Right Dorsolateral Prefrontal Cortex in the Ultimatum Game
articles.authors: Haim Assor; Jonathan slater; Eliran Halali
articles.abstract: In many social situations, a conflict exists between self-interest and social considerations such as fairness and reciprocity. Previous research suggests that self-interested behavior is an automatic response, requiring cognitive control to be regulated. Consistent with this view, neuroeconomics findings implicate the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rDLPFC) in regulating self-interested behavior and implementing social preferences. Whereas prior neuromodulation studies have shown that inhibition or disruption of the rDLPFC increases self-interested behavior, studies examining the effects of enhancing rDLPFC activity have yielded inconsistent results. Moreover, it remains unclear whether such enhancement promotes responses to intentional unfairness alone or also to inequality per se. In the present study, we applied anodal transcranial direct-current stimulation (tDCS) over the rDLPFC to reexamine its causal role in regulating self-interested behavior among ultimatum game responders. In addition, we tested whether this manipulation promotes responses to both intentional unfairness and inequality resulting from an intention-free process. The results show that anodal stimulation increased rejection rates of unfair offers, regardless of whether they were proposed by a human partner or randomly generated by a computer. These findings suggest that rDLPFC activity supports the implementation of social preferences more broadly, promoting both reciprocal fairness and inequality aversion. When considered alongside prior findings demonstrating an opposite effect of anodal stimulation applied to an adjacent lateral prefrontal region using a similar paradigm, the results point to distinct and complementary roles of lateral prefrontal regions in managing the conflict between self-interest and social preferences. We discuss implications for dual-process accounts of social decision-making.

articles.title: Seeing Through the Lens: Divergent Thinking and the Evaluation of Creative Product Designs
articles.authors: Vania Ardelia; Maryam Shahbazi; Moritz Reis; Ahmed Moustafa; Radwa Khalil
articles.abstract: Evaluations of creative products reflect both product characteristics and evaluator attributes. It remains unclear whether the ability to generate original ideas shapes how people evaluate creative products made by others. In this preregistered study, 97 university students first completed the Gough Creative Personality Scale, the openness items of the NEO Five-Factor Inventory, and a self-report item on cultural orientation. In random order, they then rated five iconic chair designs on the Creative Product Semantic Scale and completed an Alternative Uses Task with six everyday objects. The chair ratings yielded each chair's perceived originality and perceived functional quality, and a large language model scored the originality of the Alternative Uses Task responses. Divergent-thinking originality did not predict the evaluation of any chair after correction for multiple comparisons, and creative personality did not strengthen this association as predicted. Openness to experience was associated with more favorable ratings of all chairs, whereas cultural orientation, gender, hobbies, and study year were not. In exploratory analyses, the association between perceived originality and perceived functional quality varied across the five chairs. It was strongest for chairs of intermediate perceived originality, a pattern consistent with the most-advanced-yet-acceptable principle. Design features were not manipulated, so this pattern requires confirmation with larger, systematically varied sets of products. Overall, originality in idea generation was not associated with more favorable evaluations of creative products. Evaluator openness and the specific design were more closely related to these judgments.

articles.title: “What’s our color? POOR”: Exploring the Consequences of Racism-Conscious Framings of Environmental Exposures
articles.authors: Harrison James Schmitt; Lily Schwartzman; Trevor Scott Lies
articles.abstract: Environmental justice activists increasingly pursue public awareness campaigns to garner support as they face injustice. However, little psychological research has investigated the implications of different framings of recognition justice for collective action. Two experiments with qualitative components test the primary hypothesis that recognition of systemic racism in environmental exposures may represent a double-edged sword. We test implications of racism-conscious framings of inequitable lead exposures on collective action intentions among Black, Latine, and White US residents. Study 1 (n=590) finds that a racism-conscious frame increases anger and systemic knowledge of racism but does not affect collective action intentions, except among highly racially identified White participants, whose collective action intentions decreased after the manipulation. Results of Study 2 (n=703) suggest that a combined racism- and class-conscious frame may prevent (highly-identified) White disengagement from collective action. We discuss addressing environmental injustice through coalition building while acknowledging the double-edged sword of racism-conscious recognition.

articles.title: The State of Play: Methodological Reflections on Phenomenological Psychopathology
articles.authors: Jodie Louise Russell; Lucienne Spencer; Matthew Broome
articles.abstract: In this paper, we reflect on the position of the researcher within the field of phenomenological psychopathology and the ways they can overcome privilege and outsider status in order to more accurately and ethically grasp the structure of disorder experience from the perspective of the person living it. §1 discusses problems incorporating lived experience as well as its challenges within phenomenological psychopathology. §2 introduces the phenomenological notion of play in the work of Husserl and Fink. §3 elaborates on the political and ethical dimensions of play using the work of Lugones, and §4 then discusses how playfulness might be applied in health research to overcome the problems outlined in §1. §5 then gives examples of how play might be utilised within the methodology of phenomenological psychopathology. Overall, we suggest that both researchers and those with lived experience can engage in processes of understanding that can facilitate safe and inclusive interactions through the medium of play.

articles.title: Pupil Dynamics Track Preparatory Control and Selective Learning in Decision Making
articles.authors: Yifei Deng; Jonathon R. Howlett; Marcelo G Mattar
articles.abstract: A unifying theory of phasic pupil responses suggests that pupil diameter reflects information gain following an observation. However, it remains unclear whether pupil responses track information indiscriminately or selectively encode specific types of information, and whether this selectivity shifts across task phases. To address this, we developed a decision making task with information streams from three sources: control signals, decision-relevant stimuli, and decision-irrelevant stimuli. This design allowed us to dissociate pupillary responses to different forms of information gain (Shannon surprise and learning) across sources and phases. Analyzing pupillometry data from 30 participants, we found modulators of pupil responses shifted from perceptual surprise to policy-related learning over the course of trials. Furthermore, cue-related surprise drove responses immediately after its presentation and during perceptual processing of stimuli, whereas decision-relevant learning modulated responses only post-decision. These findings refine the information-theoretic framework by distinguishing automatic, surprise-related dilation from selective, learning-related dilation gated by decision relevance.

articles.title: The Measurement Reliability Crisis in Event-Related Potential Research: Evidence from Bilingual Language Control
articles.authors: Projnya Mojumdar
articles.abstract: Event-related potential (ERP) research exhibits a critical methodological blind spot: inter-condition correlations (ρXY), the parameter that mathematically determines difference wave reliability via the Lord–Novick formula, are systematically unmeasured. Classical Test Theory demonstrates that difference wave reliability is inversely related to ρXY, with high correlations suppressing reliability even when constituent waveforms are psychometrically sound. A purposive examination of four foundational ERP studies in bilingual language switching (2001–2016, Ncitations ≈ 1,575) found that none report difference wave reliability or inter-condition correlations, despite difference waves being the primary dependent variables isolating language control processes. Sensitivity analysis reveals that this vulnerability extends across the entire plausible parameter space: even moderate inter-condition correlations (ρXY = .50–.60) require constituent reliabilities approaching methodological ceilings (ρ = .85–.88) to achieve adequate difference wave reliability (ρDD′ ≥ .70). Because the observed inter-condition correlation is itself capped at √(ρXX′ρYY′), difference wave reliability is bounded between zero and the constituent reliability, and it falls to zero exactly as experimental control drives ρXY toward that ceiling: constituent reliabilities of .85 yield ρDD′ = .50 at ρXY = .70 and ρDD′ = 0 at ρXY = .85. The absence of empirical ρXY measurements means the field cannot determine whether two decades of N2 debate reflect genuine neurocognitive complexity, measurement instability, or both. Three reforms can address this gap: mandatory reporting of difference wave reliability and inter-condition correlations, adoption of Generalizability Theory frameworks, and single-trial analytical methods that avoid categorical subtraction. These principles extend beyond bilingual research to all ERP domains using difference waves. Systematic psychometric verification should precede theoretical elaboration.

articles.title: The Other Side of Prolific: Ethical Research Guidelines Based on a Mixed Methods Investigation of Prolific Platform Workers’ Experiences
articles.authors: Louis Bachaud; Macken Murphy; Antoine Marie
articles.abstract:
Experimental and survey research is increasingly reliant on crowdsourced
participant recruitment platforms like Prolific. Yet, while Prolific workers are arguably one of the
most well-studied populations in human history, little is known about their actual working
conditions. This preregistered mixed-methods study explores working conditions on Prolific
drawing on different sources: (1) a qualitative inductive analysis of the r/ProlificAC subreddit, a
platform where Prolific workers gather to discuss their experiences; (2) statistics from a survey on
working conditions, labor identity, income, motivations, fraud, and potential grievances of Prolific
workers (n=455); (3) qualitative analyses of open-ended responses to the same survey. Overall,
these analyses reveal an unbalanced power dynamic on the platform, with the workers at a
disadvantage relative to researchers, due to competition between workers, lack of social protection,
hurdles to collective organization, and platform design—logics inherent to the crowdsourcing
model. We also reveal for the first time clear evidence of fraud on the worker side of Prolific,
through a secondary market of trading and faking accounts. Based on these findings, we provide
clear and actionable guidelines for researchers wishing to use the platform in an ethical way. We
also suggest steps for the Prolific company to both ensure data quality and guarantee fair relations
between clients and workers.

articles.title: Stage 1 Registered Report: Levels and Types of Processing: Levels of Processing for Recall of Color-Object Associations After Perceptual Encoding Tasks
articles.authors: Michael Rihs; Nicolas Rothen
articles.abstract: According to the levels of processing account, memory recall improves when information is encoded at a deep rather than at a shallow level of processing. Most studies demonstrated this levels of processing effect by comparing a perceptual with a semantic type of processing for verbal material. While some studies have also demonstrated levels of processing effects using only semantic types of processing, it remains unclear whether such effects can also occur using only perceptual types of processing. The current study aims at showing a levels of processing effect for color-object associations after a perceptual type of processing. In a new orientation task, participants are asked to compare images either on a shallow (“Is the image larger than the reference image?”) or on a deep level of processing (“Does the image differ from the reference image?”). In Experiment 1, we will replicate previous findings on the processing effect in image-color associations using concrete objects within the new task framework. In Experiment 2, we will extend these findings to abstract stimuli, thereby testing the generalizability of the effect beyond semantically meaningful content. Participants are expected to show improved recall of color-image associations when they are processed on a deep rather than on a shallow level. Overall, the current study should give further insights into levels of processing theory by showing that a processing effect occurs without the involvement of semantic processing.

articles.title: Convincing Without Conflict? Persuasion and Its Social Costs in Human–AI Conversations About Meat Reduction
articles.authors: Elena Wurth; Georg Ahnert; Ira Elisa Herwig; Ahmed Salem; Markus Strohmaier; Jutta Mata
articles.abstract: Meat consumption in high-income countries exceeds recommendations. Because meals are often shared, conversations can spark meat reduction, yet advocates often remain silent because persuading carries social costs. Generative AI has proven persuasive and could inform such conversations. Drawing on research on persuasion and reactance, we examined how persuasion and its social costs depend on the source of the strategies and on the medium delivering them. In a preregistered 5 × 2 experiment (N = 521), participants discussed a shared meal with a fictional counterpart, either a chatbot or a text-based script. The counterpart used strategies from the behavioral science literature, a large language model, or a generative agent simulation, or did not argue for meat reduction (neutral and placebo controls). Arguing for meat reduction increased intentions and more than quadrupled the odds of choosing a vegetarian dish in both media; arguing for an unrelated sustainability behavior did not shift choice. Persuasion increased perceived threat to freedom but did not reduce liking of the counterpart. AI-derived strategies persuaded as well as literature-based strategies, at no higher social cost. As predicted, the chatbot incurred higher social costs than the text-based dialogue. Studies of AI-based persuasion should assess social costs alongside persuasiveness.

articles.title: The Environmental Includes the Social: On the Psychological Structure of Altruistic and Biospheric Values
articles.authors: Nicolas Eric Neef; Quinn J Hundgen; Siegmar Otto; P. Wesley Schultz
articles.abstract: Ample research discusses the relationship between altruistic (human-oriented) and biospheric (nature-oriented) values. Some propose a single, other-oriented construct. Others argue for two related but distinct constructs. Extending the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern, we propose a third position: biospheric values include altruistic values. Across three studies spanning 53 countries (Study 1: N = 222, U.S. sample; Study 2: N = 791, U.S. sample; Study 3: N = 85,796, 52 countries), we find support for this inclusion model. First, across much of the world, individuals who hold strong biospheric values also tend to hold strong altruistic values, whereas holding strong altruistic values does not imply holding strong biospheric values to the same extent. Second, biospheric and altruistic values predicted humanitarian outcomes similarly, but biospheric values predicted environmental outcomes better than altruistic values. Third, a bifactor-(S-1) model representing the Inclusion Model fit the data better than two alternatives, a unidimensional model or a correlated two-factor model. Finally, we demonstrate how modeling data in line with the Inclusion Model resolves interpretational challenges that can arise when treating both values as unidimensional (i.e., lack of discrimination) or correlated (e.g., suppression). The inclusion model advances theoretical understanding of biospheric and altruistic values. Effects commonly attributed to biospheric values may partly reflect their altruistic core. Practically, interventions targeting biospheric values may also tap into altruistic values, whereas interventions appealing to altruistic values can reach broader audiences. Future work should determine the model’s boundaries and explore global heterogeneity.

articles.title: AI versus human source attribution and perceived empathy in supportive communication: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles.authors: Arthur Bran Herbener; Filip Skjold Thidemann; Caroline Gjørtsvang Kock; Malene Flensborg Damholdt
articles.abstract: Research suggests that people attribute less empathy to supportive communication labelled as AI-generated rather than human-written, but the evidence is mixed, and it is unclear whether the effect varies with how empathy is conceptualized and operationalized. In the present paper, we report a systematic review and meta-analysis of source-attribution effects (human vs. AI) on perceived empathy in supportive communication. A systematic literature search identified 10 records reporting the results of 18 independent studies (N = 13,541). We observed a small source-attribution effect on perceived general empathy (g = 0.41, 95% CI [0.23, 0.58]), cognitive empathy (g = 0.39, 95% CI [0.16, 0.63]), motivational empathy (g = 0.42, 95% CI [0.19, 0.64]), and a moderate effect for affective empathy (g = 0.50, 95% CI [0.19, 0.81]). However, substantial heterogeneity was observed across studies. Alt-hough gender initially emerged as a significant moderator of general perceived empathy, this association was no longer significant after excluding two influential outliers. The analyses also found no statistically significant moderation by age, exposure type (vignette vs. first-person interaction), or supportive setting. Thus, the sources of the substantial between-study heterogeneity remain largely unex-plained. Future research is needed to identify the conditions shaping source-attribution effects on empathy and evaluate whether these effects persist or fade over the course of interactions.

articles.title: Feasibility of virtual reality in assessing functional communication in persons with aphasia
articles.authors: Marina Ruiter; Vitória Piai; Hilde Bosschers; Mirjam Otters; Lizet van Ewijk; Edward Bosma; Willemijn Josefien Doedens
articles.abstract: Functional communication skills represent important measures in aphasia therapy. Assessing these skills, however, remains challenging. Mainstream pen-and-paper based instruments often elicit indirect rather than direct speech and fail to capture the complex communicative demands encountered in everyday communication situations, limiting their ecological validity and construct validity. The current study explored the feasibility of using immersive Virtual Reality (iVR) to assess functional communication in persons with aphasia. After developing a proof-of-concept version – incorporating the needs and ideas of both speech and language therapists and persons with aphasia - we investigated whether (1) iVR enables a realistic simulation of everyday communication, including its technical feasibility and acceptability for the intended users, and (2)  iVR simulation has added value for functional communication assessment by allowing manipulation of communicative complexity, the elicitation of direct speech, and both verbal and non-verbal aspects of communication to be assessed. The results suggest that it is technically feasible to create iVR environments for the assessment of functional communication in persons with aphasia that are acceptable to (end) users and that enhance the construct validity of functional communication tests. Despite remaining areas for improvement, iVR was found to have a clear added value for assessment purposes.

articles.title: Risks and Benefits of Neuroticism in Adolescence: Longitudinal Evidence from Population and Clinic-Referred Samples
articles.authors: Larissa Lucia Wieczorek; Eva Bleckmann; Solomiia Myroniuk; Bertus F. Jeronimus; Sanne Booij; Jenny Wagner; Albertine Oldehinkel
articles.abstract:
Background: Neuroticism is known for being linked to detrimental outcomes, but it may also serve beneficial functions in adolescence, where avoiding and protecting oneself from risks becomes crucial. 
Method: We examined potential risks and benefits of neuroticism based on longitudinal data of two samples of Dutch adolescents, one population (n = 2229, 51% female) and one clinic-referred (n = 543, 34% female) sample. Neuroticism was measured with parent-ratings of the temperament facets fear and frustration and used to predict a diverse set of outcomes in the domains lifestyle choices (e.g., substance abuse) and social resources (e.g., social skills) between ages 11 to 19. 
Results: High neuroticism conveyed heightened risk but three key observations refine this picture: (1) fear related to fewer risks than frustration and was additionally linked to benefits regarding better social skills and more prosocial behavior among adolescents in the clinic-referred sample; (2) both fear and frustration were consistently associated with parent-rated social behavior problems across measurement points, while other risk-related associations were less consistent; (3) most links between fear and detrimental outcomes became non-significant after controlling for childhood adversity (e.g., low socioeconomic status, parental divorce). 
Conclusions: Although our results indicate several risk-related effects, we also provide initial evidence that the fear facet of neuroticism can be beneficial in adolescence, especially among youth with a clinical background and in the social domain. We call for more nuanced research studying the potential protective role of neuroticism within high-risk populations.

articles.title: Repetition and Form in Music, Poetry, and Animal Vocalization
articles.authors: Makiko Sadakata; Patrick E. Savage; Christ Billy Aryanto; Tecumseh Fitch
articles.abstract: Music is diverse across human cultures, and animal vocalisations vary across non-human species. Nonetheless, basic principles of interaction and formal structure recur across both. Music, poetry, and animal “song” exhibit structures characterised by repetition, variation, and hierarchical chunking. The degree of variation tolerated depends on style or species, creating a rich space for communicative interaction. We organise formal constraints along two continua: repetition–variation (what is repeated and varied) and choric–dialogic (whether vocalisers sing together or take turns). We argue that predictive coding explains how repetition and variation balance predictability and surprise across vocal communication. Regularities established through repetition support individual prediction, coordination, and social bonding. Drawing on the Cantometric database of vocal music across hundreds of human cultures, we find that collective singing tends to involve shorter, more repetitive phrases, whereas solo singing tends to involve longer, less repetitive phrases. We consider these findings alongside poetry and animal vocalisations to explore recurring patterns across species and cultures. We conclude that applying principles of predictive coding to repetition in formal structures across a broad comparative database yields explicit testable hypotheses and exciting insights into why both humans and animals repeat themselves, and often find repetition attractive.

articles.title: Feeling Good Sustains Acting Green: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Warm Glow and Pro-Environmental Behavior
articles.authors: Linli Zhou; Cameron Brick; Disa Sauter
articles.abstract: When we engage in pro-environmental behaviors that align with our personal values, we can experience positive feelings, known as warm glow. Theories suggest a potential positive feedback loop such that people who anticipate feeling more warm glow are more likely to act pro-environmentally, and acting in line with their personal values may in turn elicit warm glow, thereby encouraging further pro-environmental behavior. There is considerable empirical work from psychology, marketing and economics investigating these relationships, but to date this work has not been systematically synthesized. A test of the strength and robustness of the theorized links is needed to answer the question of whether warm glow is in fact consistently related to pro-environmental behavior. We report a systematic review and meta-analysis probing the robustness of the associations between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Following the PRISMA guidance, we identified 94 papers with 251 effects based on 58,313 participants. A pre-registered three-level random-effects meta-analytic model was used to estimate overall effects and to examine moderation by behavioral domain and measurement approach. The associations between both anticipated and experienced warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors were robust and medium-to-large (rs: .43 – .53). Substantial heterogeneity persisted after accounting for moderators, suggesting meaningful variation in effect sizes across studies. Overall, these findings provide strong evidence of robust links between warm glow and pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. Future research using experimental and longitudinal designs is needed to help test the causal pathways in the positive feedback loop.

articles.title: Development of a Two-Dimensional Boredom Intolerance Scale and Associations Between Boredom Intolerance and Problematic Short-Video Use
articles.authors: Zhifang Hu; YueLin; Qinxue Liu
articles.abstract:
With digital applications becoming increasingly integrated into daily life, individuals may become less tolerant of boredom. However, existing measures of boredom intolerance have primarily focused on negative emotional responses to boredom, while providing limited insight into behavioral tendencies when encountering boredom. The present study developed a two-dimensional Boredom Intolerance Scale through five studies and examined the associations between boredom intolerance and problematic short-video use.
Study 1 used qualitative interviews and grounded theory analysis to identify the conceptual domains and dimensions of boredom intolerance, revealing two dimensions: emotional intolerance and behavioral avoidance. Study 2 conducted exploratory factor analysis with 444 participants (Mage = 23.99 ± 5.41 years; 66.89% female) and developed an eight-item two-dimensional scale. Study 3 conducted confirmatory factor analysis and criterion-related validity analyses with 347 participants (Mage = 21.79 ± 3.38 years; 74.64% female), further supporting the two-dimensional structure of boredom intolerance. Study 4 employed a two-wave longitudinal design with 219 participants (Mage = 21.62 ± 2.56 years; 78.5% female) and found that problematic short-video use positively predicted boredom intolerance. Study 5 used a 14-day diary design with 185 participants (Mage = 21.13 ± 1.54 years; 85.4% female) and found that boredom intolerance positively predicted state-level problematic short-video use.

articles.title: Economic and social conservatism show a complex relationship with values of inequality and social control in an online US sample
articles.authors: Guy A. Lavender Forsyth; Ananish Chaudhuri; Quentin Atkinson
articles.abstract: Economically and socially conservative attitudes are frequently presented as stemming from distinct values about inequality and social control, respectively. However, existing research often relies on psychological scales, like Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) and Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA), that were not designed to measure values about inequality and social control directly, and which blur the boundary between values and attitudes. Here, we explore the relationship between political values and attitudes in an online USA sample (N=893), taking advantage of the new Dual Foundations Scale, which was specifically designed to measure inequality and social control values. Using multilevel Bayesian models to examine relationships at the level of individual attitudes, we find that, as predicted, values of inequality were positively associated with economic conservatism, and values about social control with social conservatism. However, associations varied across individual items, and social conservatism was overall less strongly associated with social control values than with inequality values and religious identification. Exploratory follow-up analyses indicate that whereas economically conservative attitudes cluster as expected with inequality values and SDO, socially conservative attitudes are not reliably related to social control values (or RWA’s Submission or Aggression subdimensions) and instead cluster with RWA Traditionalism, which is made up of items that some argue simply restate socially conservative attitudes. Our novel approach and findings therefore support some of the main claims of two-dimensional theories of ideology while challenging others, and suggest relationships between social conservatism, social control values, and authoritarianism are more complex than standard two-dimensional approaches to political ideology often assume.

articles.title: Construct Emergence Tracing: From Meaning to Mechanism in Transformer Interpretability via Generative Psychometrics
articles.authors: Hudson Golino
articles.abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) allow researchers and practitioners to develop and deploy systems that perform impressive feats such as generating coherent texts and answering questions across various domains. Yet, there is currently an interpretability problem regarding the internal representation of multidimensional psychological constructs (e.g., personality traits) throughout multiple layers of deep neural networks. Here, we propose Construct Emergence Tracing (CET), a novel methodology to address this problem. CET utilizes ideas from Generative Psychometrics to trace the emergence of concepts from high-level meaning to underlying mechanisms. CET consists of Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis combined with three complementary indices reflecting the quality of representation (semantic coherence via normalized mutual information; NMI, entropy-based organization structure via Total Entropy Fit Index; TEFI, and topological compressibility via a compression-based proxy for Kolmogorov Complexity; KC). CET also computes a weighted composite of the above three indices in order to derive a metric named Representational Maturity (RM). We applied CET to fourteen LM models ranging from nominal sizes of 117 million to 32 billion parameters. We utilized a fixed design of five items per attribute representing the five attributes of grandiose narcissism and yielded a total of 9,801,000 network estimates across recorded states, embedding dimensions, and repeated item samples. Results show that across architectures construct recovery generally increases from early to intermediate states. However, its initiation, amplitude, alignment with different metrics, and termination vary considerably across models. Across Qwen2.5-Instruct, overall mean NMI followed a monotonic increase based on nominal model size from 0.504 (0.5B) to 0.653 (32B). This trend did not replicate for selected peak values or output layer retention. Furthermore, the final state was divided into two distinct patterns of behaviors: (a) five models showed zero or close-to-zero mean NMI (GPT-2, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B); (b) nine models maintained final state mean NMI within 0.504-0.777 range. Lastly, we observed no consistent convergence in the optimal layers regarding peak semantic coherence, optimal entropy fit, and maximal representational maturity. Overall, we demonstrated that both the number of parameters and the extraction from the output layer alone do not suffice in capturing abstract representations inside LMs. Through CET, researchers and practitioners obtain macro-level estimations of construct organization trajectories across different layers.

articles.title: A review of perceived social traits in AI-generated hyperrealistic human faces
articles.authors: Dalia Israel; Genevieve Quek; Manuel Varlet; Tijl Grootswagers
articles.abstract: Advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI) produce synthetic human faces that are difficult to distinguish from photographs of real people. Because social impressions from faces form rapidly and can influence consequential judgements, the growing realism of AI-generated faces raises questions about how these faces are socially perceived. This review synthesises evidence from 10 empirical studies examining whether AI-generated faces are evaluated differently from real faces and what may account for these differences. Across the reviewed studies, AI-generated faces receive more favourable social evaluations than real faces, including higher ratings of trustworthiness and attractiveness, while familiarity also emerges as a component of their perception. These patterns are consistent with established face-perception research showing that faces perceived as more typical tend to receive more favourable social evaluations. AI-generated faces may disproportionately reflect such characteristics, including greater averageness or typicality. However, appearance alone does not determine these judgements: disclosure, labelling, and beliefs about artificiality can weaken or alter otherwise favourable impressions. Overall, social responses to AI-generated faces appear to reflect an interaction between perceptual characteristics and beliefs about origin. The central challenge is no longer only whether AI-generated faces can pass as human, but how people who do not exist can shape real social judgements.

articles.title: Hierarchical knowledge and skills undermine payoff-biased social learning
articles.authors: Nanda Ramo Jafarian; Björn Lindström; Ingmar Visser; Annemie Ploeger; Pieter van den Berg; Lucas Molleman
articles.abstract: Acquiring skills and knowledge (“traits”) through social learning is central to human development and cultural evolution. Yet it remains unclear how individuals can effectively learn from others when traits form hierarchies, with advanced traits building on more basic ones. We present a model showing that trait hierarchies favour “proximal social learning” where individuals copy others who are only slightly more knowledgeable. In contrast, payoff bias - often assumed to be universally advantageous - performs poorly because it directs learners toward advanced traits they lack the basics for. Our experiments demonstrate that people indeed shift to proximal social learning when conditions favour it. Our results challenge core assumptions of mainstream cultural evolution theory and highlight that trait hierarchies are a key factor shaping human social learning.

articles.title: From Knowing to Doing: ADHD and the Enactment of Chronic Pain Self-Management in Youth—A Conceptual Review
articles.authors: Mahdieh Vaezbarenji; David Moore; Edmund Sonuga-Barke
articles.abstract: Young people with chronic pain are routinely asked to carry out multicomponent self-management plans with limited day-to-day support. ADHD traits are common, and often unrecognised, among young people attending paediatric pain services, yet little is known about how an ADHD profile shapes the way they act on these plans. This conceptual review argues that some apparent non-adherence in this group reflects a knowing-to-doing gap: a mismatch between the demands of treatment plans and the executive and motivational profile associated with ADHD, rather than a lack of knowledge or concern. Drawing on ADHD, prospective memory, paediatric chronic illness, and health-behaviour research, we identify where this mismatch is most likely to occur: remembering to act at the right time, starting without a prompt, monitoring progress, and resuming after interruption. As direct evidence is lacking, we set out testable propositions: executive differences predict enactment beyond knowledge and intention; the gap widens when plans require independent organisation and narrows with external structure; and inconsistent enactment contributes to later pain-related disability. Clinically, services should identify where enactment breaks down before attributing it to low effort, and adapt plans through simpler actions, routines, prompts, and coordinated home–school–clinic support.

articles.title: Widely Used, Unevenly Evaluated? Generative AI Use, AI-Output Evaluation, and Their Association with Socioeconomic Background Across 59 Countries (PISA 2025)
articles.authors: Eileen Richter; Sebastian Röhl; Joshua Weidlich; Luisa Köhler; Ada Jung; Korbinian Moeller; Markus Spitzer
articles.abstract: Generative AI chatbots have become part of 15-year-olds' schoolwork. However, it is less clear whether these students also evaluate what these systems produce. Using PISA 2025 data from more than 500,000 students across 59 countries, we examined how often students are asked in class to evaluate AI output, who is asked, and how closely the practice is associated with students' AI use. On average across countries, 57.5% of students used AI chatbots for schoolwork at least weekly, yet only 35.3% reported being asked often or very often to evaluate the quality of AI output in class, whereas 33.2% reported being asked never or almost never. Interestingly, students who used AI more often also reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, in all countries (pooled r = 0.34). Yet, 25% of at-least-weekly users still reported no or almost no AI-output evaluation. Furthermore, students from more advantaged socioeconomic backgrounds reported being asked more often to evaluate AI output, independent of their level of AI use. Overall, students reported being asked to evaluate AI output less often than to evaluate online information. Yet, the association of AI use with evaluation was substantially stronger for AI-output than for online-information evaluation. In sum, many students who use AI regularly report few opportunities to evaluate its output in lessons, and these opportunities are socially stratified, extending an established pattern of digital inequality to generative AI.

articles.title: Heterogeneity in reading comprehension predicts semantic context effects beyond dyslexia status
articles.authors: Elisa Gavard; Marine Royer; Eddy Cavalli
articles.abstract: Many adults with dyslexia understand texts well despite persistent word reading difficulties, and sentence context has been proposed as a compensatory resource. We tested whether contextual facilitation during word reading reflects a benefit for reading comprehension, or reliance on context driven by slow word identification or by limited semantic knowledge. Fifty-one French-speaking young adults (22 with dyslexia, 29 typical readers) read a target word aloud after four words forming a related or a control context, in semantic and syntactic conditions. Reading comprehension (without a time limit) and reading efficiency were assessed with standardized tests. Dyslexia status was strongly associated with reading efficiency (r = −.70) and only weakly with reading comprehension (r = −.22). Context facilitated naming in both groups. In proportion to naming latency, an equivalence test excluded a group difference in facilitation larger than about 12 ms; in raw milliseconds, facilitation was larger in adults with dyslexia, who were slower overall. Semantic facilitation was larger in readers with lower reading comprehension (27 vs. 14 ms at 1 SD below and above the mean), mainly among those with the lowest scores. This relation was specific to semantic context and held when reading efficiency and dyslexia status were taken into account. Reading efficiency did not modulate proportional facilitation, but the comprehension and efficiency slopes did not differ significantly. We suggest that semantic facilitation indexes reliance on context, not a benefit for comprehension, and that compensation in adult dyslexia should be tested in individuals, against reading comprehension.

articles.title: Metaphorical cost: Processing of metaphorical and literal language in people with Alzheimer’s disease
articles.authors: JAN EDSON RODRIGUES LEITE
articles.abstract: Whether metaphorical language is processed differently from literal language remains an open question: lesion and imaging studies have pointed to partly distinct neural substrates, whereas reading-time studies have found comparable costs when context is supportive. This study examines the question in speakers of Brazilian Portuguese with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), a condition that affects both semantic and visuospatial abilities, and asks whether the conceptual content of a sentence, spatial or non-spatial, modulates processing cost independently of metaphoricity. Forty-two participants (14 with AD, 14 healthy elderly and 14 healthy young adults) read twelve sentences in a 2 × 2 design (metaphorical or literal; spatial or non-spatial) on a tablet and judged an inference about each of them. Accuracy, reading times and response times were recorded. The AD group was less accurate and slower overall. Spatial sentences were read more slowly by all groups. Metaphoricity interacted with group in reading times: only the AD group read metaphors more slowly than literal sentences, and this cost was concentrated in metaphors with a spatial source domain. Spatiality interacted with group in response times, although comparisons within groups were not significant. The results indicate that the cost attributed to metaphor depends on the population tested, on the stage of processing that is measured and on the conceptual domain recruited by the sentence. They do not support a general processing disadvantage for metaphorical language.

articles.title: Actual use of generative AI chatbots for mental health advice across adulthood: Psychological correlates and the moderating role of age
articles.authors: Angeliki Triantafillaki; Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Panagiota Peleka; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: Little is known about which adults actually turn to generative artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots for mental health advice, and whether the profile of these users changes with age. The aim of this study was to examine the sociodemographic and psychological correlates of actual chatbot consultation for mental health advice, and of its frequency. In this cross-sectional online survey, 843 Greek adults aged 18 to 50 years reported whether, and how often, they had consulted an AI chatbot about their thoughts and feelings during the previous three months. Validated instruments captured anxiety, depression, loneliness, sleep quality, self-esteem and problematic social media use. Logistic and proportional odds models, extended with age-by-predictor product terms, were fitted. Seven in ten respondents (71.3%) reported such use, and 37.5% did so weekly or more often. Independent correlates of any use were younger age, recent consultation with a mental health professional, greater problematic social media use and lower self-esteem. Among users, worse sleep, lower self-esteem and greater problematic social media use were associated with more frequent consultation of AI chatbots for mental health advice. Age moderated the role of loneliness, which was related to chatbot use only among the youngest respondents, and a comparable but weaker gradient emerged for depressive symptoms. Chatbot-based mental health advice is now widespread among Greek adults up to midlife. Clinicians should ask patients of every age about it, and preventive efforts should recognize that its psychological drivers are not uniform across adulthood.

articles.title: Gender and Agency in AI Career Guidance for Women: A Socio-Technical Audit of General-Purpose Language Models
articles.authors: Sara Portell Fonolla; Yasmina El Fassi
articles.abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. Studies of gender bias in large language model (LLM) career advice mostly score single outputs about a person described to the model. But career guidance is a conversation with the woman herself, in which the advice can end up making the decision for her or treat a barrier she faces as a lack of confidence. We report a preregistered socio-technical audit of the career guidance that ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give women through their APIs. We scripted 34 multi-turn conversations grounded in research on women’s careers, ran each five times per system, and added male versions of 14 to test gender cues (972 conversations). Human raters scored 304 conversations on nine objectives drawn from that research and from coaching ethics, with a second rater and an expert adjudicator for disagreements. Failures to preserve her agency had the highest share for every system (36% to 50% of conversations scored 1 or above on a 0 to 3 scale) and were more frequent than gender bias failures. Gemini was more often sycophantic. Swapping the user's gender showed no systematic difference, but pair differences depended on how the name was given. No LLM judge agreed acceptably with human raters, and the human raters also often disagreed, so the rates are descriptive. Audits of AI career advice should use more than one gender cue and, because models change, be repeated over time. LLM judges can serve as a screening aid, but scoring needs two or more human experts.

articles.title: What the Tally Hid: Screening Live-Observation Codes for Saturation, Floor Effects, and Degeneracy Before Piloting
articles.authors: Vince Jacques de Blauwe; Antonio Fidalgo
articles.abstract: Observational coding instruments are usually judged by their summary score, yet a well-distributed total can hide codes that cannot discriminate between units. We set out a pre-piloting screening protocol for live-observation coding sheets and calibrate it on a worked case. In 15 stranger dyads, a ten-code sheet produced a healthy-looking composite (M = 26.63, SD = 9.64), yet four engagement codes ran at 74–94% of their protocol maximum, three withdrawal codes sat at 0–8%, and only three codes varied in a graded way between dyads. Resampling the deposited counts, the all-code conjunctive rule detected this pattern in 100% of pilots from N = 2 to 15, but against a no-pathology null it raised false alarms in 33.1% of pilots at N = 2 and 9.2% at N = 4, falling below 5% only from N = 6. Excluding the never-observed monologue and silence codes, detection was flat and non-monotonic (90.8% at N = 4; 87.0% at N = 6). Threshold distance and code degeneracy, not pilot size, govern whether screening succeeds. We therefore recommend reporting each code’s percentage of maximum, between-unit variance and signed distance to the nearest threshold, rather than a pilot N. A closed-form margin index built from these quantities, z = d√N/SD, reproduced the simulated code-level results to within 1.2 percentage points on average from N = 4 and is released as an R function. The protocol and its two principles are provisional and unregistered, pending replication on a second bin-level dataset; all counts come from a single non-blinded coder.

articles.title: Inward-directed utterances and the evolution of language
articles.authors: Conor Houghton
articles.abstract: At some point in our evolutionary history humans gained the ability to communicate using language. Most accounts of language evolution focus on its role in communication. This review proposes an alternative: that the decisive step was the internalisation of utterance as a tool for directing thought. A hierarchy of animal communication is developed to sharpen this proposal. Evidence from the development of language in children supports the view that internalisation is central to language acquisition. The success of chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models provides a further, independent demonstration of the importance of language as a tool. These proposals together suggest that language is patterned on the structure of thought rather than shaped primarily by the demands of communication.

articles.title: Retrieval-Augmented Virtual Patients for Eating Disorders
articles.authors: Carlo Smaniotto Mantovani; Wagner de Lara Machado; Bolivar Ramos Cibils Filho; Regis Kopper; Gabriel Balke dos Santos; Joao Ricardo Nickenig Vissoci; Márcio Sarroglia Pinho
articles.abstract: Background: Language models can generate fluent virtual patient dialogue, but its clinical plausibility requires evaluation. Objective: We describe a locally deployed simulator for anorexia nervosa, bulimia nervosa, and binge-eating disorder and examine the perceived realism of its responses. Method: A Unity application links a three-dimensional avatar to Llama 3 8B. A retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) configuration uses Nomic Embed Text and ChromaDB to retrieve clinical material. Six raters from psychology or nutrition assessed 45 Brazilian Portuguese responses to 15 questions under three conditions: Llama 3 8B without RAG, Llama 3 8B with RAG, and GPT-4o. Each response received six ratings on a five-point realism scale, yielding 270 ratings. Comparisons were descriptive, and agreement was assessed using quadratically weighted Gwet’s AC2. Results: Mean realism was 3.81 without RAG, 3.76 with RAG, and 4.65 for GPT-4o. Observed agreement was 83.5%, with AC2 = .60. Qualitative comments emphasized clinical plausibility concerns without RAG and language quality concerns with RAG; error frequencies were not quantified. Conclusions: RAG was not associated with a higher overall realism mean in this response set. Clinical plausibility and linguistic naturalness warrant separate assessment in a comparison that controls generation settings. The study did not evaluate avatar effects, multi-turn coherence, safety, or learning outcomes.

articles.title: Prejudice against Northeastern Brazilians in the dual-process motivational model
articles.authors: Felipe Vilanova; Angelo Brandelli Costa; Tiago Jessé Souza Lima; Luana Elayne Cunha Souza; Taciano L Milfont
articles.abstract: We examined how prejudice against Northeastern Brazilians fits within the structure of generalized prejudice and how it relates to right-wing authoritarianism and social dominance orientation. We reanalyzed online questionnaire data from four Brazilian samples comprising 1,679 participants. Attitudes toward Northeastern Brazilians were positive on average. Negative attitudes correlated most strongly with prejudice against derogated groups (pooled correlation of .46), followed by prejudice against dissident groups (.37), and showed a near-zero association with prejudice against dangerous groups. Factor analyses largely supported alignment with derogated groups. Social dominance orientation had a stronger independent association with negative attitudes than right-wing authoritarianism. The results indicate that prejudice against Northeastern Brazilians most closely resembles prejudice directed at groups perceived as socially subordinate.

articles.title: Characterizing deaf and hard-of-hearing language experiences as arousal-regulation processes
articles.authors: Christina Kim; Laurel Aichler; Onudeah Nicolarakis; Shilpa Hanumantha Lacy; Rachel Sortino; Rachel Pizzie
articles.abstract: Empirical language research with deaf and hard-of-hearing (DHH) groups often includes proficiency, age of acquisition, or language background measures but excludes people’s socioemotional context. Measuring socioemotional context depends on characterizing the socioemotional experiences associated with DHH language development and use. We used the biopsychosocial model of arousal regulation as a theoretical lens to explore 11 qualitative interviews with DHH participants. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we developed three characteristic themes: 1) Deafness is not a monolith, 2) Name it to tame it – Language Anxiety, and 3) Positive roots for resilient shoots. These themes show that DHH language experiences are heterogeneous, that negative experiences can represent language anxiety, and that positive experiences modulate arousal regulation. Our study highlights new socioemotional considerations for language processing research like how emotions influence language use, how motivations support language skills, and how communication strategies impact social interactions within DHH communities.

articles.title: Subjective and objective socioeconomic status as predictors of midlife cognition in the rural Deep South: the Bogalusa Heart Study
articles.authors: Jade E. Jenkins; Amy Thierry; Ileana De Anda-Duran; Shakira Suglia; Lydia Bazzano; Owen Carmichael
articles.abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Lifecourse socioeconomic conditions influence Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias (ADRD) risk. Higher objective socioeconomic status (O-SES) is consistently associated with better later life cognition and lower ADRD risk. One’s perception of their socioeconomic status, or subjective socioeconomic status (S-SES), is a robust predictor of myriad health outcomes.
