However, it’s utility as a predictor of cognition in aging populations is not well characterized and has yet to be investigated in the Deep South, a historically underrepresented region characterized by socioeconomic disadvantage and elevated ADRD risk. 
METHODS: O-SES and S-SES were examined as predictors of cognition in the Bogalusa Heart Study. We derived O-SES using confirmatory factor analysis and measured S-SES using the country ladder from the MacArthur Scale of Subjective Social Status. Exploratory analyses were conducted to test for potential effect measure modification by sex and race. 
RESULTS: O-SES, but not S-SES, was associated with cognition in the full sample. Exploratory analyses revealed a small positive association between S-SES and cognition only for White men, which was attenuated after accounting for O-SES. The relationship between O-SES and cognition was not modified by sex and race.
DISCUSSION: Our finding that higher O-SES is associated with better cognition is consistent with extensive evidence. However, we did not replicate previously found associations between S-SES and cognition observed in other older populations and with numerous other health outcomes. Given the paucity of research in the rural Deep South, more work is needed to understand S-SES and ADRD risk in this setting.

articles.title: Social media addiction is associated with poor mental health, AI chatbot use, and problematic digital behaviours among Generation Z: a cross-sectional study in Greece
articles.authors: Aglaia Katsiroumpa; Angeliki Triantafillaki; Panagiota Peleka; Parisis Gallos; Ioannis Moisoglou; Olga Galani; Maria Tsiachri; Petros Galanis
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE To examine the association between social media addiction and mental health among members of Generation Z in Greece. Moreover, we examined the association between social media addiction and social media-related behaviours. METHOD We conducted a web-based cross-sectional study with a convenience sample of 599 individuals aged 18 to 29 years. We measured social media addiction with the Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale. Outcomes were anxiety, depression, loneliness, social media fatigue, sleep quality, life satisfaction, physician visits for mental health issues, artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot use for mental health issues, second-screen use, social media distraction, fear of missing out, and no-social-media phobia. We performed multivariable logistic regression analysis adjusting for sex, age, and financial status, and we examined interactions between social media addiction and these variables. RESULTS Overall, 56.6% of participants were addicted to social media. The prevalence of anxiety was 57.5% among addicted participants and 38.1% among non-addicted participants, while the prevalence of depression was 39.2% and 25.8%, respectively. After adjustment for confounders, social media addiction was associated with higher odds of anxiety, depression, loneliness, social media fatigue, poor sleep quality, life dissatisfaction, and AI chatbot use for mental health issues. Also, social media addiction was associated with higher odds of second-screen use, social media distraction, fear of missing out, and no-social-media phobia. Sex, age, and financial status did not substantially modify these associations. CONCLUSIONS Social media addiction is highly prevalent among Generation Z and is associated with several mental health problems and problematic digital behaviours. Interventions to prevent social media addiction and to facilitate access to professional mental health care among young people are needed.

articles.title: Covert control over the real-time dynamics of human interactions with Ducksoup
articles.authors: Pablo Arias Sarah; Guillaume Denis; Philippe schyns; Rachael Jack; Petter Johansson; Lars Hall; Jean-Julien Aucouturier
articles.abstract:
Uncovering how facial and vocal signals shape social interactions is difficult because researchers
cannot control how humans behave during free conversations. Here we demonstrate that recent
advances in AI-based transformation filters enable researchers to have covert experimental control
over the real-time dynamics of social interactions. We introduce Ducksoup, a scientific
videoconference platform that allows researchers to collect social interaction experiments online,
realistically transform participants' faces and voices in real time mid-conversation, record the
synchronized interactions and extract multimodal time series from recordings for analysis. In a
preregistered experiment (N = 64 participants), we replicate recent laboratory findings in a fully
online setup: artificially aligning participants’ smiles increased mutual enjoyment while remaining
undetected. The paradigm also revealed feedback effects on participants’ spontaneous facial, vocal
and verbal behavior. By combining the ecological validity of free interactions with experimental
control and scalable data collection, Ducksoup turns natural conversations into a causal
experimental paradigm for psychology and neuroscience.

articles.title: How to Measure Victimhood and Moral Judgment with the Theory of Dyadic Morality
articles.authors: Emily Kubin; Kurt Gray
articles.abstract: The Theory of Dyadic Morality (TDM) argues that moral condemnation revolves around intuitive perceptions of victimization. We provide a curated collection of items for measuring moral judgment and perceived victimization, organized around one question: “From someone’s perspective, who is victimizing whom, how, and to what extent?” Each part of the question connects to a core element of our moral psychology, including the dyad itself (an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable victim), the continuum of perceived victimization (mild to severe), different kinds of victimization (e.g., physical violence versus spiritual suffering), and the important worldviews that shape perceived victimization (e.g., cultural and politics). We show how classic paradigms, from moral dilemmas to moral dumbfounding, can be measured with TDM, and we outline future directions, including how TDM can align artificial intelligence with human moral judgment.

articles.title: Cultural Distance between Geographic Regions is associated with Lower Mobility, Weaker Democracy, and Increased Risk of Civil Conflict
articles.authors: Cindel J. M. White; Michael Muthukrishna
articles.abstract: Stable nations require strangers to coordinate and cooperate despite cultural differences. Using the Cultural Fixation Index (CFST) on World Values Survey data (268,992 participants; 95 countries; 2005–2022), we quantify cultural distances between demographic groups within countries, including between regions, ethnicities, religious groups, education levels, and social classes. We test whether within-country cultural distances are associated with national indicators of social mobility, democracy, and civil conflict. A pre-registered multiverse analysis (54,600 model specifications; 100 model families; 6 demographic groupings; 6 outcome measures) shows that only cultural distance between geographic regions is associated robustly with institutional weaknesses, such as higher corruption, weaker democracy, lower social mobility, and greater risk of civil conflict. In contrast, distances between ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic groups show few significant associations with national indicators of governance, mobility, and conflict, and educational distance is often associated with lower corruption and stronger democracies. The results imply that what matters is not diversity per se, but whether culturally distinct groups are geographically segregated.

articles.title: Structural Equation Modeling with Word-Embedding for Text-Based Measurement
articles.authors: Artur Pokropek; Hubert Plisiecki; Maria Flakus; Adam Waszkowski; Kinga Małyska; Tomasz Żółtak
articles.abstract:
In recent years, advances in natural language processing have led researchers to increasingly use
text-based data to study various psychological and social phenomena. This usually goes without
an explicit measurement model or evaluation of the psychometric properties of text-based
indicators. We introduce SEM-WE, which fits measurement and structural models to correlation
matrices that are based on word embeddings derived from texts under study. Each construct is
represented by several indicator words or phrases. The centered cosine matrix provides the input
for estimating loadings, residuals, model fit statistics, reliability indicators, and parameters
describing relations between constructs. We use a synthetic corpus, a survey study that combines
both textual and Likert-type questions, and real-life posts from X in a multi-study validation
exercise. Using simulated persona attitudes, self-ratings, and human coding as benchmarks, we
compare six approaches: dictionary stance counts, embedding centroids based on positive
indicators alone, embedding centroids contrasting positive and negative indicators, annotations by
a local language model, annotations by a frontier language model, and SEM-WE. SEM-WE
reproduces benchmark signs in these examples and their ordering at least as well as other methods,
matching or outperforming most competitors under the reported configurations. Dictionary and
centroid results vary more across reported configurations, while large language models perform
well in the synthetic and survey studies; however, at much higher computational cost.

articles.title: Navigating Dynamic Risks: Outcome Monitoring and Evaluation under Escalating Risk
articles.authors: Corinna Lorenz; Nicola Kristina Ferdinand
articles.abstract:
Real-world risk-taking unfolds through sequences of decisions where stakes escalate incrementally. Yet most ERP research examines isolated outcomes, leaving neural processing of accumulating risk poorly understood. We developed an ERP-adapted Columbia Card Task enabling precise temporal analysis of feedback processing across consecutive outcomes, systematically manipulating gain amounts, loss amounts, and loss
probability while recording EEG in 25 participants. We measured early outcome detection via the feedbackrelated negativity (FRN) and reward positivity (RewP) and later evaluative processing via the P3b.

Early outcome processing tentatively depended on the potential loss amount. FRN amplitudes differentiated between
positive and negative outcomes when large losses were at stake but not when losses were small, an effect carried by more pronounced responses to negative outcomes under large losses. The RewP showed a similar but less well supported pattern. Gain amount and loss probability did not modulate early components, and we found no evidence that they changed across the feedback sequence. In contrast, the P3b was larger for negative than for positive outcomes, and this difference increased across the feedback sequence as risk accumulated, without evidence for a dependence on the stakes. Exploratory analyses did not provide consistent evidence that individual risk propensity modulated these patterns.

With early processing scaling with the consequences at stake and later evaluation increasingly focusing on negative outcomes as the feedback sequence progresses, these findings suggest that outcome monitoring under escalating risk is not a fixed response to outcome valence.

articles.title: Auditory-perceptual deficits and speech illusions are associated with psychotomimesis in an NMDA receptor antagonist model of schizophrenia
articles.authors: Ursule Taujanskaite; Georges Iskandar; Vaughan Bell; Sunjeev Kamboj
articles.abstract: Hallucinations are a core symptom of psychosis. Predictive processing accounts suggest that hallucinations arise from an imbalance between sensory evidence and prior expectations. Given the role of glutamatergic dysfunction in psychosis, the NMDA receptor antagonist nitrous oxide (N2O) may provide a model for investigating hallucinatory experiences. This pre-registered study (https://osf.io/4jhsx examined the effects of N2O on subjective and behavioural indices of psychosis-like (hallucinatory) phenomena. Healthy participants were randomised to 50%-N2O (n=80) or medical-air (n=40) and completed the Psychotomimetic States Inventory (PSI) before and during gas inhalation. False alarms, hits, and exploratory signal detection indices from the white noise (speech illusions) task were compared between N2O and medical-air. Mediation of drug effects on canonical signal detection metrics – perceptual sensitivity and response bias – via change in psychotomimesis (ΔPSI) and sedation was also examined. N2O administration was associated with fewer hits but no change in false alarms, reflected in reduced perceptual sensitivity and more conservative response bias. Larger ΔPSI was associated with more false alarms in the N2O group; ΔPSI (particularly positive psychotomimesis; ΔPSI-Positive) also mediated the effect of drug condition on perceptual sensitivity, while sedation and negative psychotomimesis did not have a reliable indirect role. Susceptibility to NMDA receptor antagonist-induced anomalous perceptual experiences and deficits may rely on or be preceded by subjective psychotomimetic effects. However, the unexpected pattern of reduced perceptual sensitivity and conservative response bias under N2O challenges the notion that reduced perceptual sensitivity following NMDA-receptor antagonism would necessarily lead to hallucination-like responding.

articles.title: Positive Affect is Associated with Interactive Social Media Use: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles.authors: Evelyn Alice Halliday Murray; Daniel Shaw; Jisun Kim; Andrew Jones; Charlotte Rebecca Pennington
articles.abstract: Research examining associations between social media usage (SMU) and adolescent psychological wellbeing has relied on cross-sectional self-report data, limiting understanding of specific social media behaviours and within-person variability. To address these limitations, the present study combined an objective experimental task with Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) to investigate associations between adolescents’ SMU styles, momentary affect, and trait depressive symptoms. 229 older adolescents (110 females; Mage = 22.60, 18-25 years old) completed the Social Networking Site Behaviour Task, which classifies SMU along a passive to interactive continuum, across three days (573 datapoints). Trait depressive symptoms were assessed on Day 1 using the Maryland Trait and State Depression Scale, while momentary affect was measured on each day using the International Positive and Negative Affect Schedule. Linear mixed-effects models revealed between-person variability in SMU style. Positive affect was significantly associated with more interactive SMU (liking and commenting relative to scrolling), whereas negative affect and trait depressive symptoms were not significantly associated with SMU style. Our findings suggest that SMU styles reflect both stable individual differences and dynamic within-person variation associated with positive affective states. This demonstrates the value of combining objective behavioural measures with longitudinal EMA design to advance understanding SMU and psychological wellbeing.

articles.title: Exploring Environmental Structure for Task-general Representation Learning
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract:
Humans are always facing new tasks, but they are not forced to solve them from scratch, since
they are almost always able to leverage previous experience to scaffold current learning. We
propose that what connects past to present is task-general representations: abstract knowledge of
the structure shared across tasks that serves as a foundation for new learning. Treating tasks
performed in the past as samples from an unknown task distribution, we review how properties
of the observed samples shape task general representations. We apply the same lens to two
different timescales; learning over the course of minutes to days and development over the
course of months to years. We then consider how people exert control over their own task
distributions. We propose that exploration, by diversifying experience, keeps task-general
representations adaptive because people choose their experiences using the very representations
they are learning, errors in those representations can become self-sustaining. Specifically, we
highlight directed and value-free random exploration as two distinct exploration strategies that
correct different distortions in task-general representation.

articles.title: A thalamocortical mnemonic model of consciousness: thalamic selection of conscious content
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Dominant theories of consciousness (Higher-Order, Global Workspace, Integrated Information and Predictive Processing theories) locate its neural substrate in cortical association areas. I argue that this convergence reflects the technical accessibility of cortical tissue rather than a demonstrated sufficiency of cortical circuits, and I present the Thalamocortical Mnemonic Model of Consciousness (TMMC), which assigns the thalamus a constitutive role in selecting and sustaining conscious content. Content is selected by competition at the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) among thalamic channels, under four selection pressures with identifiable anatomical sources: salience, prediction, value and mnemonic coherence. The mediodorsal nucleus (MD) sustains prefrontal activity once content has arrived, the hippocampus generates episodic endogenous content, the nucleus reuniens coordinates its arrival in prefrontal cortex, and the amygdala biases the competition directly. Building on earlier constructive accounts, the TMMC holds that all conscious content is a configuration of learned cortical patterns; its contribution is the mechanism that selects among them. The model distinguishes two partially dissociable state variables, the level, L(t), and the content, C(t), of consciousness, and three operating modes (exogenous, endogenous and free) whose transitions reflect coupled thalamocortical processes on multiple timescales. Three falsifiable predictions are derived: thalamic precedence over prefrontal cortex for spontaneous thought, accelerated loss of maintained content without delayed generation after MD damage, and thalamus-to-cortex theta-band flow before perceptual switches in binocular rivalry. A further test asks whether the selection pressures dissociate. The TMMC offers a mechanistic alternative to corticocentric models and a research program for thalamocortical consciousness science.

articles.title: Impossibility and Logical Contradictions Can Enhance the Perceived Value of Fictional Theological Propositions
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Supernatural concepts are often thought to gain cultural attraction by violating intuitive expectations in limited ways, but many theological doctrines also involve logical contradictions or impossibilities. It remains unclear how such formal violations influence people’s evaluations of religious propositions. In the present study, 96 Japanese adults rated 20 fictional theological propositions on dimensions related to perceived value, including importance, profundity, interestingness, sacredness, and shareability. Those propositions were rated for impossibility and logical contradiction. A composite positive-evaluation score was derived from items rating perceived value and analyzed using linear mixed-effects models. The result shows higher impossibility and higher logical contradiction predict higher positive evaluations of the propositions. These findings suggest that impossible and contradictory theological content can be positively evaluated.

articles.title: Examining HiTOP Through Naturalistic Symptom Descriptions in Anonymous Online Mental Health Forums: A Mixed-Methods Study Protocol
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Background: The Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology (HiTOP) organises covarying symptoms and maladaptive traits into transdiagnostic dimensions to address limitations of categorical diagnosis. Naturalistic symptom descriptions may complement structured assessments. Objective: This protocol describes a reproducible mixed-methods workflow to derive symptom indicators from forum posts and examine their organisation relative to HiTOP. Methods and analysis: The target sample is 80,000 public Reddit posts. After local de-identification, a large language model (LLM) will extract symptom labels and supporting paraphrases. Two human experts will independently review outputs for up to 250 posts. Three embedding models will flag potentially equivalent symptom labels for local LLM assessment. Two experts will qualitatively review the most frequent canonical symptom labels (at least 1,000) and develop a codebook of symptom categories, continuing until a prespecified saturation criterion is met. An LLM will assign canonical symptom labels to these categories, producing binary post-level indicators. Multiverse-inspired structural analyses will compare network, component, factor, and clustering representations across discovery, internal tuning, and holdout partitions. Evaluation will assess interpretability, stability, and agreement with expert mapping to HiTOP. Supplementary analyses will include agent-assisted exploration, codebook application to DepressionEmo and the Reddit Mental Health Dataset, and pooled integrative analysis that may include additional comparable corpora.
Discussion: The study will examine whether symptom co-expression within posts forms interpretable patterns corresponding to HiTOP.
Ethics: The Ethics Committee of Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin approved the study (EA2/274/25). The study was preregistered on 8 May 2026 (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00040244).
Keywords: Hierarchical Taxonomy of Psychopathology, natural language processing, large language models, Reddit, mixed methods, study protocol

articles.title: Counting on Suppression: Does Learning to Ignore Distractors Depend on Executive Resources? A Registered Report
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Observers can learn to suppress the locations where salient distractors tend to appear, so that distractors at these locations are less likely to capture attention. This learned distractor suppression is thought to depend on an automatic mechanism that does not require working memory resources. However, previous dual-task studies in this literature have often asked participants to retain or manipulate information that was tested after search, which does not necessarily engage executive processes during learning. In the present study, we will test more directly whether learning to suppress a distractor location depends on executive resources. To do so, participants will perform an additional singleton task while counting the targets that contain a given line orientation, a concurrent executive task integrated into the search itself. We will compare this load group with a no-load control group that will perform the same task without the concurrent task. We hypothesise that the suppression effect will be smaller in the load group than in the control group (H1). Moreover, if this form of learning requires executive resources, the suppression effect could be absent in the load group (H2). The results will show whether learned distractor suppression is independent of executive resources, or whether previous null results reflect secondary tasks that left these resources available during search.

articles.title: Let’s protect us Europeans from them: Emotional predictors of outgroup solidarity, ingroup defense, and outgroup derogation in response to the Ukrainian war (2022 – 2025)
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: The Russian invasion of Ukraine has threatened Europe’s safety and economy. Europeans responded with solidarity towards Ukrainians, demonstrated ingroup strength, but also expressed derogatory attitudes towards Russians and mistrusted public media. To investigate how emotional states of anxiety, anger, and being moved were linked to threat perceptions and intergroup responses, we conducted three cross-sectional studies (Ntotal = 690, March 2022, March 2023, May 2025) among German-speaking Europeans. Results from a multilevel path-model (second level variable: year), showed threat perceptions to be positively linked to anger and being moved (realistic and symbolic threat), and anxiety (realistic threat). Anger and being moved predicted solidarity with Ukrainians and defense of the European ingroup, while anger and anxiety predicted derogation of the Russian outgroup. Interestingly, feelings of being moved were negatively associated with outgroup derogation and media mistrust, supporting being moved as a collective approach emotion binding Europeans together while reducing negative consequences. [Note: This manuscript is currently under peer review. Content and formatting may change during the review process.]

articles_hidden.title: How should Moral Motivation be Represented? The Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA)
articles_hidden.authors: Paul McKee; Gregory Russell Samanez-Larkin; Scott A. Huettel; Walter Sinnott-Armstrong
articles_hidden.abstract: Moral psychology has mostly asked which motives drive moral action, and rarely how moral motivation should be represented once several are active at once. Most theories represent it as a single dominant motive or as one continuum from bad to good. Both discard information: a person torn between strong competing motivations and a person who feels nothing occupy the same position. We argue that representational format is a testable empirical claim, not a modeling convenience, and propose the Motivation of Moral Action (MoMA), which represents moral motivation as four independent dimensions formed by crossing motivational direction (approach, avoid) with perceived moral valence (good, bad). MoMA does not specify which motives matter; it specifies the space in which they combine. We derive requirements for an adequate architecture, show that lower-rank representations necessarily collapse psychologically distinct states, and state predictions distinguishing MoMA from simpler alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: Coordinated Psychological Intervention Ensembles Outperform Single-Mechanism Designs Across Societal Challenges
articles_hidden.authors: Anandita Sabherwal; Danielle Goldwert; Madalina Vlasceanu; Elke U. Weber
articles_hidden.abstract: Behavioral science tends to seek the single most predictive explanation for behavioral phenomena and subsequently the most effective intervention for behavior change. Yet many consequential outcomes, from climate action to democratic attitudes, result from multiple psychological processes, raising the question of whether combining interventions that leverage different processes would prove more effective. Across a 13-intervention megastudy and a second, megastudy-informed experiment (Ns = 8,488 and 2,547 US adults; both quota-matched and preregistered) we test whether intervention ensembles—deliberate combinations of distinct psychological modules delivered together—can more effectively shape target behaviors and attitudes.  We test three principles for constructing such ensembles: 1) outcome optimizing ensembles (combining top-performing individual interventions), 2) mechanism coverage ensembles (covering key psychological drivers of the outcome), and 3) multi-level synergy ensembles (combining individual-, collective-, and system-level processes). Ensembles consistently outperformed their constituent single-mechanism interventions. In Study 1, relative to an informed control, the strongest ensemble increased climate policy support by 41.5% and donation by 43.0%. And in Study 2, the ensemble was significantly more effective than its components in reducing partisan animosity and strengthening democratic attitudes. The largest gains were achieved by multi-level synergistic ensembles that aligned processes across individual, collective, and systemic levels. LLM-assisted analyses of participant reasoning reveal that effective ensembles work by resolving complementary psychological barriers, not by simply providing more arguments. For complex societal challenges shaped by multiple barriers, interventions can achieve behavior change at greater rate and scale by designing coordinated intervention ensembles rather than by searching for the single best mechanism.

articles_hidden.title: Legislative Inconsistencies in Defining Psychology Registration in the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld): Mandatory Reporting and Implications for Provisional Psychologists
articles_hidden.authors: Daniel Paul Sullivan
articles_hidden.abstract: 2021 amendments to the Criminal Code Act 1899 (Qld) in Queensland to criminalise the non-disclosure to police of child sexual abuse (CSA) (s229BC) had consequential implications for the practice of psychology, particularly psychotherapy. Where patients make self-disclosures about current or historical CSA perpetrated against them by an adult when they were a minor (including historical CSA in a now adult patient), psychologists, like all adults in Queensland are required to report that to police, unless one of the “reasonable excuses” against disclosure applies. This paper discusses the wording in the Act with a focus on relevant reasonable excuses in the therapy context, and how the Act contains ambiguity in the application of the law to psychology trainees who are provisional, rather than student registrants under the national health practitioner regulatory scheme.

articles_hidden.title: Error correction necessitates immediate, answer-containing feedback: Challenging error suppression, episodic reinstatement, and semantic mediation accounts
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Folger; Matthew Rhodes; Jexy An Nepangue; Hannah Hausman
articles_hidden.abstract: Generating errors during learning benefits subsequent recall, particularly when corrective feedback is presented immediately. Feedback in existing research conflates notification of error commission with provision of the correct target. Across two experiments, we examined the effects of immediate feedback, delayed feedback, and delayed feedback with an immediate “error” warning on cued and error-cued recall. In Experiment 1, warnings did not mitigate the detrimental effect of delayed feedback on cued recall, indicating that optimal pretesting requires immediate, answer-containing feedback. This challenges two hypotheses of errorful learning: that suppressing errors at encoding facilitates error correction (the error-suppression hypothesis), and that error commission promotes context binding which enables episodic reinstatement during feedback and at test (episodic reinstatement hypothesis). Immediate feedback improved cued recall performance but not participants’ ability to recall the accuracy of their initial responses, further contradicting the possibility of episodic reinstatement at test facilitating target recovery. In Experiment 2, delaying feedback improved error-cued recall, undermining mediator-based accounts which assume that errors function as additional retrieval cues, increasing the likelihood of successfully retrieving the target. We propose that error commission increases attention to the target at encoding, strengthening the cue–target retrieval route.

articles_hidden.title: I Remember That Question: Using Eye Tracking to See How Prequestions Shape Reading
articles_hidden.authors: Jason Geller
articles_hidden.abstract:
Answering questions before learning (prequestions) improves memory for the information they
address, but how it does so is unclear. A common proposal is that prequestions direct attention to
that information. We tested this account by recording eye movements while participants read a
text about polio and tuberculosis after answering prequestions about one topic or none, so that
every target sentence was read both with and without prequestions. Prequestions improved
memory only for the prequestioned information, and eye movements showed the same
specificity. Ex-Gaussian models, which separate typical reading time from occasional unusually
long readings, showed that prequestions did not change typical reading of the answer sentences.
Instead, these sentences received more unusually long readings, were looked back to more often,
and were re-read for longer; other sentences were unaffected. Prequestions thus guide attention
selectively rather than heightening it, consistent with additional processing when readers
recognize an answer.

articles_hidden.title: Measuring bilingual vocabulary: A systematic review and meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Alvin Wei Ming Tan; Federica Moro; Gianmatteo Farabolini
articles_hidden.abstract: Bilingual vocabulary size is often compared with monolingual scores, especially when bilingual normative data are not available, but there is no agreement on how to measure it. Bilingual scores commonly rely on a single language score, on the total amount of words known across languages (total vocabulary) or on the sum of concepts known in either language (conceptual vocabulary). We conducted a Bayesian network meta-analysis comparing these three bilingual measures against monolingual scores, and analyzed the effect of age, vocabulary domain (receptive and expressive), instrument type (direct or parent-report), language development status and language distance. Out of 3747 records retrieved from ERIC, PubMed, PsycInfo, and Google Scholar, we included 226 studies reporting data on 50,020 children. Conceptual vocabulary did not credibly differ from monolingual scores (g = −0.08, 95% CrI [−0.38, 0.21]), whereas total vocabulary was larger and single-language vocabulary smaller. Across age, total vocabulary moved further from monolingual scores and single-language vocabulary moved closer to them, while conceptual vocabulary showed no reliable change. Bilingual-monolingual differences were more negative for expressive than for receptive vocabulary across bilingual measures, and direct tests widened the gap for single-language scores only. Language development status and language distance had no reliable effects, but both were sparsely sampled. When bilingual vocabulary size has to be compared with the monolingual one, conceptual vocabulary is the closest measure. Evidence remains limited beyond the age of six, in clinical populations and for language pairs that do not include English.

articles_hidden.title: Engagement Trajectories in a Jail-Based Dialectical Behavior Therapy Group
articles_hidden.authors: Lindsay Stall; Edelyn Verona
articles_hidden.abstract: Jail-based mental health interventions are delivered under conditions of short and unpredictable stays, making treatment engagement difficult to evaluate. Although Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) has demonstrated promise in correctional settings, little is known about how engagement changes over time in jail-based DBT. Participants (N = 325; 84.9% male) were enrolled in a six-week, jail-adapted DBT skills group as part of a larger randomized controlled trial. Facilitators provided weekly ratings of attendance, in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion. Latent Profile Growth Modeling identified engagement trajectories among participants who attended at least three sessions (N = 232), and mixed-effects models examined whether profile membership predicted changes in mental health symptoms and coping. Participants attended an average of approximately 6 of 12 sessions, and 40.2% completed the full cycle. Noncompletion occurred through multiple routes, including release or transfer and the program’s three-miss attendance criterion. Three trajectories were identified: Declining Engagement (37.5%), High-Stable Engagement (29.7%), and High Early Engagement with Drop-Off (32.8%). The High-Stable group had the highest attendance and completion rate. The Declining group showed lower in-session participation, homework completion, and diary card completion beginning early in treatment, whereas the High Early Engagement with Drop-Off group remained relatively engaged across these indicators before a later decline in attendance. Noncompletion in the latter group was primarily associated with release or transfer. Profile membership was not associated with differential changes in symptoms or coping, although mental health symptoms and maladaptive coping decreased overall. These findings show that repeated engagement measures can distinguish early, broad declines in participation from later interruptions in attendance that would be obscured by completion status alone.

articles_hidden.title: Leveraging Consensus-Based Ratings to Assess Dimensions of Early Life Adversity: Links to Emotion Regulation and Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Mark S. Chen; Alexis Brieant; Isabella Kate Kate Peckinpaugh; Leila Adames; Ante Dany; Dylan G. Gee
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Dimensional models of early life adversity (ELA) posit distinct developmental consequences of threat, deprivation, uncontrollability, and unpredictability. Existing approaches force each event into a single dimension or rely on self-ratings that may conflate exposure with subjective appraisal.
Objective: We evaluated consensus-based dimensional ratings as an alternative and examined their associations with emotion regulation and psychopathology.
Participants and Setting: A Prolific sample (N=200; Mage=23.06; 49.5% female; 48% racial minorities) was used to derive the consensus values; a community sample (N=291; Mage=22.40; 59.5% female; 60.5% racial minorities) was used to test their transportability out of sample.
Methods: In Sample 1, we derived consensus values from averaged ratings of 82 ELA items and compared consensus-based and self-rating scoring (feasibility test). In Sample 2, we applied Sample 1 consensus values (transportability test). Dimension scores—threat, deprivation, unpredictability, uncontrollability—predicted cognitive reappraisal, emotion dysregulation, and psychopathology symptoms.
Results: Uncontrollability and unpredictability were highly collinear with threat and deprivation (VIFs > 50) and thus not retained in regression models. Consensus-based scoring was feasible in Sample 1, and consensus-based associations transported to Sample 2. Deprivation was associated with depression, PTSD, and emotion dysregulation in both samples (R² = .04-.22, ps < .01), and negatively with cognitive reappraisal (p = .007).
Conclusions: ELA dimensions are separable at an event level but entangled at the person level, preventing clean specificity in naturalistic samples noted in the literature. Consensus-based values may offer a way to select samples with distinct exposure profiles, treat self–consensus discrepancies as meaningful appraisal differences, and evaluate whether such appraisals could be intervention targets.

articles_hidden.title: Inconclusive prospective effects between psychological monitor competency and mental health literacy: A reassessment of Guo et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Guo et al. recently reported statistically significant links in a cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) model and interpreted these findings as evidence that psychological monitor competency reinforces mental health literacy among university psychological monitors. However, methodological research has shown that cross-lagged estimates may emerge as artifacts of model specification rather than reflecting genuine prospective influence. To examine the robustness of the reported findings, we reanalyzed the data used by Guo et al. using several alternative analytic approaches. Across specifications, estimated associations varied considerably in both magnitude and direction, with positive, negative, and nonsignificant effects all observed. Meta-analytic aggregation of estimates across models generally yielded effects that were not statistically different from zero. These results indicate that the conclusions advanced by Guo et al. may not be robust and that the apparent prospective associations could be attributable to methodological artifacts. Strong developmental interpretations are therefore not warranted on the basis of the available evidence. We recommend that observational findings, including cross-lagged effects, be evaluated across multiple defensible modeling approaches before substantive conclusions are drawn.

articles_hidden.title: The Approximate Number System is an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison
articles_hidden.authors: Attila Krajcsi
articles_hidden.abstract: The approximate number system (ANS) is an imprecise representation of numbers that is widely assumed to support both symbolic and nonsymbolic numerical tasks. It is believed to be not only the foundation for simple numerical operations but also for higher-level mathematical thinking. One fundamental support for the ANS is the existence of the ratio effect in symbolic number comparison. That is, for example, when Arabic numbers are compared, human performance is proportional to the ratio of the to-be-compared values, similar to psychophysical comparison of perceptual features. A critical issue with this account, however, is that an exact operation, which is required in symbolic number comparison, cannot be backed solely by an imprecise representation. This is for several reasons. First, while a psychophysical model assumes imprecise representation, humans can compare symbolic numbers with arbitrarily high precision. Second, psychophysical models predict worse performance for number pairs with a relatively small ratio than the actual human performance. Third, if an additional mechanism supporting exact comparison is also assumed, current empirical evidence cannot verify the ANS model. Fourth, the ANS account differentiates approximate and exact tasks, where only approximate tasks can be solved purely with the ANS. However, the comparison task is assumed to be processed purely by the ANS, even if the task is exact. Taken together, these arguments make the ANS an unlikely account for symbolic number comparison. While these arguments question the role of the ANS in symbolic number processing, the ANS may have a role in nonsymbolic number processing, although the general relevance of the ANS may be considerably lower than assumed by previous works. Consequently, the individual differences in the sensitivity of the ANS may be less critical in higher-level math performance, dyscalculia diagnosis, or training programs.

articles_hidden.title: The Family Criticism Paradigm: A Laboratory Task for Investigating Psychophysiological Responses in Parent–Child Triads
articles_hidden.authors: Matias M. Pulopulos; Nadischa Helena Dierdorp; Melanie De Leener; Mariah Matar; Michel Sfeir; Sien Verelst; Shiyao Wang; Federico Cassioli; Guy Bosmans; Eva Ceulemans
articles_hidden.abstract: Investigating stress regulation processes within the family context offers important evidence to understand the development of mental and physical health problems. However, laboratory paradigms for investigating stress in several family members simultaneously are limited. The present study introduces and evaluates a standardized paradigm to investigate psychophysiological responses to family-framed standardized evaluative feedback in parents and children simultaneously. A total of 120 families (consisting of a mother, father, and their child aged 10-12 years) participated in a laboratory session in which they were individually but simultaneously exposed to neutral, praising, and critical audio comments presented as originating from the other two family members. Psychophysiological response was assessed using mood, state rumination, and autonomic nervous system activity measures, including vagally mediated heart rate variability (HRV), pre-ejection period (PEP), and skin conductance level (SCL). Results showed that criticism increased negative affect (tension, sadness, anger) and decreased positive affect in both parents and children. Self-critical rumination increased 5 and 10 min after the exposure to the paradigm. At the physiological level, HRV was lower during both praise and criticism than during neutral comments, indicating reduced parasympathetic activity during social evaluation. During recovery, HRV increased, suggesting a rebound in parasympathetic activity, while sympathetic responses showed decreased cardiac sympathetic activity (PEP) in parents and increased sympathetic activation (SCL) in children. These findings support the use of this paradigm for eliciting affective, cognitive, and physiological stress responses among family members, offering a promising approach for research on stress regulation and resilience within family systems.

articles_hidden.title: Ambiguity Preferences Are Distinct from Beliefs About Risk
articles_hidden.authors: Syed Farhad Ali Shah; Jeffrey B. Dennison; James B. Wyngaarden; John A. Clithero; David Victor Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: Debates across the behavioral sciences have long examined whether ambiguity avoidance in decision making reflects stable preferences for certainty or uncertainty in beliefs formed through limited experience. Prior studies have commonly used the max–min expected utility (MMEU) model to interpret ambiguity-related decisions, but MMEU confounds preferences with beliefs by focusing on the range of possible probabilities rather than how individuals form them. We conducted two experiments (N = 53; N = 298) using a Linked Colored Lottery Task to test whether ambiguity avoidance reflects stable preferences or beliefs about outcome distributions. Participants first learned to associate colors with distinct outcome distributions by sampling from them and then made incentivized choices between options that varied in ambiguity. This design allowed us to observe how beliefs about distributional variance influenced decisions and to distinguish whether choices reflected belief construction versus uncertainty evaluation. We compared models based on MMEU and on subjective recursive expected utility (SREU), which explicitly separates beliefs from preferences. In both experiments, model comparison favored SREU, and participants with more dispersed inferred beliefs were more likely to avoid ambiguous options. Sampling patterns and memory for probabilities showed similar effects. Apparent age-related differences in ambiguity avoidance were also better explained by belief variance than by preferences. These results suggest that ambiguity avoidance often reflects perceived imprecision in learned beliefs rather than an inherent aversion to uncertainty, plausibly a cognitive rather than affective phenomenon, with implications for understanding decision making across learning, memory, and uncertainty processing domains.

articles_hidden.title: Reconstructing Dörner's 2003 PSI island agent: trace-level validation and implementation-dependent behaviour
articles_hidden.authors: Alec Sproten
articles_hidden.abstract: Dörner's PSI theory treats motivation, emotion and cognition as one regulatory system and was implemented as an agent that lives on a simulated island. The aim of this paper is to open that program, version 4.9.1.200 of 2003, to inspection. We report a reconstruction in Python and its validation against the original running under Wine. For one complete reference life of 739 behaviour cycles, the reconstruction reproduces every compared observable: all 109,140 lines of the activity protocol, all 2,802 actions with their ages, all 43 process counters and the end-of-life files, and the first 75,000 random draws agree in value and call site. In eight further lives every observed difference traces back to a single cause, a byte of a heap address that the original reads as part of a direction name; in four of them this byte changed a decision after 310 to 663 cycles. Whether the two programs produce the same distribution of behaviour has therefore not been tested. Tracing each random draw to its source exposed properties that the published description does not contain, among them a rule for background goals that inverts the rule stated in Dörner's book, side effects of the user interface on memory and time, and unguarded pointer accesses that stalled 3 of 100 reconstructed reference lives. Removing these properties together lowered deaths from 11.95 to 9.35 per 1,000 cycles over 97 paired lives. In this world one need, the collection of nucleotides, held control in 99.9 % of the recorded motive decisions.

articles_hidden.title: On the Stability of Individual Differences in the Truth Effect
articles_hidden.authors: Selina Zajdler; Lena Nadarevic; Markus Wache; Martin Schnuerch
articles_hidden.abstract: Repeated information is judged as more valid than new information, a robust cognitive phenomenon known as the truth effect. Individuals differ in the extent to which they show the effect, but results regarding the covariation of these individual differences with dispositional variables have been inconsistent. To address these inconsistencies, we focus on the methodological prerequisites necessary to find such associations: that individual differences in the truth effect can be reliably measured and that they are stable over time. We address both prerequisites across four studies using a Bayesian hierarchical model and Bayes factor model comparison. We first reanalyze three existing datasets and find mixed evidence for stability: one dataset yields inconclusive results alongside low reliability, another provides evidence for stability across sessions, and a third provides evidence for stability across retention intervals, though with considerable uncertainty regarding the magnitude. In a new experiment (N = 196, L = 50 trials per condition) designed in accordance with previously established experimental design recommendations, we then assess stability both across sessions and retention intervals within a single study. We demonstrate that individual truth effects can be reliably measured within a single session, directly validating these design recommendations, and find strong evidence that individual differences covary substantially across two sessions and retention intervals. Together, these findings lay the foundation for future research on individual differences in the truth effect and how they relate to personality traits, cognitive abilities, and other dispositional variables.

articles_hidden.title: Corruption Perceptions Predict Conspiracy Beliefs More Strongly in Low-Corruption Contexts
articles_hidden.authors: Sinan Alper; Ayşenur Düzgün; Eylül Deran Atalay; Onurcan Yilmaz
articles_hidden.abstract: Perceptions of institutional corruption are consistently associated with conspiracy beliefs, yet their predictive value may depend on the institutional context in which they arise. We propose a context-sensitive account in which corruption perceptions and distrust in institutions are more strongly predictive of conspiracy thinking in relatively clean societies than in highly corrupt ones. In Study 1 (N = 3,401), an illustrative two-country comparison in which recruitment mode and sample composition differ alongside corruption, perceived corruption was more strongly associated with conspiracy beliefs in the UK than in Türkiye, a higher-corruption context, even after accounting for theoretically-relevant individual differences. Study 2 (N = 34,356 across 20 European countries) extended this contextual moderation through a partial replication using multilevel models and institutional distrust as a proxy for perceived corruption, a related construct. The interaction with institutional distrust remained consistent across alternative models, country-level covariates, and tests of measurement invariance. These findings suggest that the belief that institutions are corrupt (Study 1) and institutional distrust (Study 2) might carry different implications depending on institutional context. By integrating individual perceptions with institutional conditions, this research advances a context-sensitive account of conspiracy beliefs.

articles_hidden.title: Contrast merger in the perception and production of bilingual speakers
articles_hidden.authors: Caihong WENG; Alexander Martin; Martijn Wieling; Ioana CHITORAN
articles_hidden.abstract:
In this study, we examine two Mandarin fricative contrasts that are variably merged in Quanzhou Southern Min–Mandarin bilingual speech. The Mandarin /f/∼/x/ contrast contains a sound /f/ that is absent from Southern Min but that can be assimilated to /hw/, making it distinct from /x/. The Mandarin /s/∼/ʂ/ contrast contains a sound /ʂ/ that is entirely absent from Southern Min and can only be assimilated to /s/. We compare speakers’ perception and production patterns for these two contrasts and and ask whether the two are related at the level of the individual speaker. Results show that /f/∼/x/ was more accurately discriminated and produced than /s/∼/ʂ/. This asymmetry is consistent with the way the two contrasts map onto the Southern Min inventory, with the acoustic and articulatory differences between them, and with the different social meanings they carry. At the individual level, however, the correlation between perceptual and production accuracy was small and below our adopted significance threshold.
The strength of this relationship did not modulated by contrast, vowel context, generation, or Mandarin usage. Perception and production therefore agree at the group level on which contrast is harder, but a speaker who perceives a contrast more accurately is not reliably the speaker who produces it more accurately.

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Differences in How Experiential and Observational Learning Shape Memory
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Children’s ability to learn and form memories through direct experience and observation increases with age. However, the development of the underlying mechanisms, particularly prediction errors (PEs), through which both learning modes influence memory, remains unclear. Using an incidental memory paradigm, we compared children (8–10 years) and adults (18–30 years) in how reward PEs (RPEs) during experiential and observational reinforcement learning affect episodic memory. Although children showed weaker learning performance, both age groups remembered images better after experiential than after observational learning, and they did not differ in recognition accuracy. However, adults showed greater memory strength and remembered images better when they or another player gambled for rewards, especially when associated with positive RPEs. In contrast, children recognized images better when they rejected gambles, and exploratory analyses linked better memory to larger unsigned RPEs when they accepted gambles. These findings suggest age differences in how one’s own and observed decisions, and potentially associated reward predictions, shape episodic memory.

articles_hidden.title: Are psychedelic users less susceptible to visual illusions? Evidence from the Illusion Game
articles_hidden.authors: Dominique Makowski; Marco Sperduti; Oliver Collins; Lucie Daudé; Joy Zogheib; Ewen Kervadec; Bruno Roméo; Pascale Piolino; Baptiste Fauvel
articles_hidden.abstract: Classic psychedelics are thought to relax prior expectations, which should weaken visual illusions. Evidence is scarce, especially outside the acute state, and error rates, the usual measure of illusion sensitivity, also depend on overall performance. We tested 118 adults, of whom 44 had never used a classic psychedelic, 39 had used one within the last 30 days (the "afterglow" period) and 35 longer ago. They completed the Illusion Game, a response-time task of judging which of two targets is larger while the strength of an illusion (Ebbinghaus, Müller-Lyer, vertical-horizontal) varies independently of the real difference between them. A hierarchical drift diffusion model was fitted to every choice and response time. Both user groups set wider decision boundaries than naïve participants, gathering more evidence before responding, and made fewer errors. We then computed an index of illusion sensitivity independent of overall accuracy: the effect of illusion strength on performance relative to that of the real difference. This index was 22% lower in users on average, equally in recent and past users, and unrelated to age, language, student status, psychological flexibility, distress or the intensity of the last experience. It correlated moderately across illusions, less than general performance did. Psychedelic users appeared somewhat less sensitive to illusions, as relaxed priors would predict, but the absence of a clear link with use recency limits interpretative confidence and generalizability.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-linguistic regularities in pronominal number neutralisation are not reflected in learning biases: Synchronic, diachronic, and experimental evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Carmen Saldana; Chundra A. Cathcart; Jessica K. Ivani; Balthasar Bickel; Mora Maldonado
articles_hidden.abstract: Although number neutralisation—the loss of singular-plural distinctions—is relatively rare in paradigms of personal pronouns, it is the most common pattern of pronominal syncretism cross-linguistically and exhibits systematic asymmetries across person values. Number distinctions are most frequently neutralised in third person, less so in second person, and least often in first person. While this generalisation has been widely noted, its empirical foundation to date remains relatively weak, and no clear mechanistic explanation has been established for why this typological asymmetry might arise. To address this gap, we investigate whether cross-linguistic patterns of number neutralisation might reflect biases in learning, such that patterns that are easier to learn are more reliably transmitted over time and consequently become more prevalent across languages. We first conduct a large-scale synchronic analysis of pronominal paradigms (1,243 languages), confirming a frequency-based hierarchy (3rd > 2nd > 1st) but challenging its previously assumed implicational nature (1st > 2nd > 3rd; i.e., if in 1st, then in 2nd, and if in 2nd, then in 3rd). A diachronic phylogenetic analysis suggests a tendency towards greater stability of number neutralisation in the order 3rd > 2nd > 1st. Overall, however, it provides limited support for the frequency-based hierarchy and no clear support for the implicational hierarchy. Finally, an artificial language learning experiment testing the learnability of different neutralisation patterns reveals that learners do not mirror typological tendencies: contrary to predictions—and in line with an author-based bias—first-person number neutralisation appears to be most learnable. These findings suggest that the typological evidence for the number neutralisation hierarchy might not be as robust as previously assumed, and that learning biases alone might not straightforwardly explain the typological tendencies. This challenges the link between learning biases and typological distributions, suggesting that pronominal paradigms evolve in a manner that is less constrained by learning biases, and/or that alternative processing and communicative biases may better account for cross-linguistic distributions of pronominal number neutralisation.

articles_hidden.title: Learning Finnish through English: The role of linguistic distance, exposure, and affective factors in L2 grit
articles_hidden.authors: Natalja Ulrich; Nils Jaekel
articles_hidden.abstract: Sustained effort and perseverance are essential for successful language learning, particularly in contexts where learners face linguistically demanding target languages such as Finnish, taught in L2 English. This study examined the role of linguistic background, language exposure, and emotional factors in explaining variation in L2 grit among 82 early-stage learners of Finnish as a foreign language. Participants completed an online survey assessing linguistic background, exposure to Finnish, language learning enjoyment, anxiety, and L2 grit. Hierarchical linear regression analyses showed that greater linguistic distance to English was consistently negatively associated with lower Finnish L2 grit, while linguistic distance to Finnish became a negative predictor after controlling for exposure. The number of previously learned languages was positively associated with L2 grit. Among exposure-related variables, Finnish media use, but not time spent in Finland, was associated with Finnish L2 grit. Language learning enjoyment emerged as a strong positive predictor, whereas anxiety was not. The findings suggest that perseverance in early-stage Finnish learning is shaped not only by the target language itself but also by multilingual experience, instructional language accessibility, and positive emotional engagement.

articles_hidden.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
articles_hidden.authors: Isabel Berwian; Yongjing Ren; Sashank Pisupti; Jialing Ding; Seohyun Moon; Jamie C. Chiu; Deepta Chandrasekhar; Yael Niv
articles_hidden.abstract:
Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis-
orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms
underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a
novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories—
to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they
uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative
models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul-
tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental
health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition-
ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi-
ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety
disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu-
lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted
interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return
of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as
a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

articles_hidden.title: Environmental Sensitivity Moderates Negative Affect During Brief Virtual Nature and Urban Exposure in Japanese Young Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Hiromi Nakadaira; Yuichi KIKURAKU; Shuhei Iimura
articles_hidden.abstract: Immersive virtual reality offers a way to experience natural settings when direct access to nature is limited. We investigated short-term affective and physiological responses to virtual natural and crowded urban environments and whether these responses differed by environmental sensitivity. Fifty-eight Japanese university students aged 18–24 years were randomly assigned to watch a 7-minute head-mounted-display video of a forest and stream (Nature, n = 29) or a crowded urban station (Urban, n = 29). Negative affect and salivary α-amylase activity were measured before and after viewing; heart rate variability was assessed during exposure. Negative affect decreased after nature exposure but increased after urban exposure. The between-condition difference in change was larger at higher levels of environmental sensitivity, driven more clearly by greater negative-affect increases in the urban condition than by sensitivity-related change in the nature condition. No statistically reliable condition difference was detected for salivary α-amylase or during-exposure heart rate variability. These findings suggest that brief immersive virtual environments elicit contrasting short-term affective responses that vary with environmental sensitivity, while physiological effects remain uncertain.

articles_hidden.title: The CEOs Who Won't Be Measured: Access, Self-Other Gaps and Working Hours in a Preregistered CEO-Team Study
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Asking a CEO's team to rate the CEO is the most direct way to test how long working hours relate to leadership, and it is the step many CEOs decline. In a preregistered study, invitations reaching an estimated 60,000 or more people produced 90 CEO responses; 49 eligible CEOs of firms with 10 or more people completed a 24-hour time grid and a 12-item Leadership Behavior Inventory. Only 15 produced the three or more team ratings the design required, against a target of 300. First, access was the binding constraint: 43% of eligible CEOs did not hand over a usable team list, those who withheld reported about eight more weekly hours (p = .09), and none of the 10 CEOs above 58 hours reached the analysis. Second, CEOs ordered their strengths and weaknesses much as their teams did (median rank correlation .60) but rated themselves higher on three of four behaviors (composite +0.28 on a 5-point scale, 95% CI [−0.02, 0.59]). An apparent concentration of that gap on weaknesses did not survive a split-half check for regression to the mean, and the preregistered compression test for minimization could not have detected it. Third, team-rated effectiveness declined with CEO hours across the observed 30- to 58-hour range (p = .037), with no detectable threshold, though the result is fragile to single clusters. With a small sample of mostly small and mid-sized firms, likely tilted toward CEOs open to feedback, these are signals, not confirmed effects. I set out the design changes needed to test them.

articles_hidden.title: Mental Sampling in Social Judgment: Examining Variability in Judgments for the Self, Close, and Distant Others
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: A growing number of theories explain various aspects of cognition through processes of mental "sampling." Under these theories, judgments (e.g. predicting whether a friend will be late) are accomplished by generating and aggregating samples, through simulation or memory retrieval. Here, we examined a key prediction of these theories: that the variability of judgments will be lower when more samples can be drawn. We test this with a novel intervention in a simple social inference task, examining people's ability to judge the probability of various everyday behaviors, comparing judgments made for themselves versus others. Responses were more consistent when predicting their own behavior than that of an acquaintance, suggesting a greater number of samples could be drawn. Surprisingly, we found only a weak relationship between the time spent with a target and the variability of estimates, suggesting that sampling processes may not rely only on retrieval from memory.

articles_hidden.title: Anhedonia and Emotional Processing of Past- and Future-Directed Mental Representations: Behavioral and Event-Related Potential Evidence
articles_hidden.authors: Matthias Pillny; Kai Härpfer; Hannes Per Carsten; Anja Riesel; Julia Klawohn; Tania Marie Lincoln
articles_hidden.abstract: Anhedonia may involve difficulties generating affective value from remembered and imagined positive experiences rather than a generalized reduction in immediate pleasure. However, its association with emotional processing across direct stimulus exposure, memory retrieval, and prospection, including the role of negative affect, remain unclear. This preregistered study examined neural and subjective emotional responses in 48 nonclinical adults with varying levels of anhedonia. Participants viewed positive, negative, and neutral images, recalled them, and imagined future experiences involving their content. During 4,000-ms trials, late positive potential (LPP) amplitudes were assessed from 400 to 4,000 ms, alongside subjective affect and imagery vividness ratings. Anhedonia was assessed using the Snaith–Hamilton Pleasure Scale. Linear mixed-effects models tested associations between anhedonia and LPP amplitudes across valence conditions and time windows, as well as subjective ratings across valence conditions. During recall, higher anhedonia was associated with reduced positive–neutral LPP differentiation at 1,000–2,000 and 2,000–3,000 ms, alongside lower pleasantness ratings for positive memories. Valence-dependent LPP associations were not significant during encoding or prospection. These findings suggest that altered affective processing of positive memories may be relevant to anhedonia, alongside broader differences in emotional responding and the vividness of mental representations.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Initial Validation of a Brief, Transdiagnostic Measure of Conflict Resolution Difficulties and Ineffective Relational Strategies
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Considerable research in recent decades has focused on developing measures assessing transdiagnostic dimensions, including measures that target dimensional symptoms rather than traditional diagnostic categories. Furthermore, a sizeable literature has focused on assessing social-cognitive vulnerabilities (e.g., experiential avoidance) thought to be linked to an array of symptoms and functioning difficulties, and a range of measures of transdiagnostic, social-cognitive vulnerabilities have been developed. However, few of them include item content directly assessing conflict resolution difficulties and ineffective interpersonal relational strategies, which also are linked to a range of psychopathology and are targeted in cognitive-behavioral and third-wave treatments. We address this gap in the transdiagnostic assessment literature by presenting initial validation data for a measure of ineffective interpersonal strategies across three studies and four samples of participants (N = 301 adults; N = 808 adults self-identifying a mental health diagnosis; N = 368 undergraduate students; N = 226 community adults). Analyses based on these samples spanned evaluation of participant perspectives on item face validity, quantitative examinations of internal structure, test-retest stability, and evaluating validity associations with a range of self-report and interview measures. Results collectively support the initial validation of an efficient interpersonal measure, the 6-item Transdiagnostic Ineffective Relational Strategies Scale (TIRSS), which is provided in appendix materials for free use for research purposes. We discuss future validation steps to build from this work, as well as ideas for sharpening interpersonal and transdiagnostic assessment research more broadly.

articles_hidden.title: The Phenomenology of Non-Ordinary Experiences during Spiritualist Séances
articles_hidden.authors: Everton de Oliveira Maraldi; Ricardo de Oliveira Souza; Juliana Almeida; Ronald Fischer; Maria Eduarda Ismerio Moreira de Oliveira; Vitor de Oliveira Moura da Silva; Luiz Augusto de Queiroz; Amanda Sales Cafezeiro; Marina Saraiva-Mendes; Tiago Bortolini
articles_hidden.abstract:
Non-Ordinary experiences (NOEs), such as feelings of unity with God, hearing voices, and sensing the presence of deceased persons, are prevalent in the general population. They may be life-transforming but are also associated with pathological conditions such as psychosis and dissociation. However, little is known about how cultural appraisals and religious practices shape their phenomenology and psychological impact in non-clinical populations. For the most part, their socio-cognitive and emotional features remain unexplored. The purpose of this study was threefold. Firstly, to investigate the phenomenological characteristics and types of NOEs reported by self-defined spirit mediums from a spiritualist home circle in the city of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Secondly, to explore the role of social context in interpreting and shaping NOEs. Finally, to gain a better understanding of the phenomenological similarities and distinctions of experiences reported in spiritualist contexts with psychopathological constructs such as dissociative and psychotic symptoms. The study used a mixed-methods approach, combining ethnographic observations of spiritualist séances, thematic content analysis of reports of séance-related NOEs, and standardized scales assessing dissociation, absorption, psychotic symptoms, symptoms of common mental disorders, and satisfaction with life. We analyzed a total of 151 independent reports of NOEs provided by a group of mediumship practitioners participating in regular séances over a period of one year and five months. The reports tapped a variety of experiences including intense emotional states (e.g., happiness, gratitude), alterations in consciousness (e.g., feelings of spacing out), spontaneous mental imagery (e.g., visions of the spiritual world), sensory-perceptual experiences (e.g., hearing voices or other unusual sounds), somatic manifestations (e.g., body tremors), and unusual experiences involving the séance table (e.g., vibrations). The experiences reported were episodic, controllable, and restricted to the séances. Overall, they were described as pleasant or innocuous. Mediums generally reported perceiving their lives as satisfying and meaningful and scored similarly to the general population on items indicative of common mental disorders. Given their cultural impact and predominantly positive effects, these experiences bear implications for differential diagnosis, and the role of cultural and religious factors in mental health, wellbeing, and cognition. The spiritualist séance provide a natural environment for observational and experimental studies of intentionally induced non-ordinary states of consciousness.
Keywords: non-ordinary experiences, dissociative experiences, psychotic experiences, psychosis continuum, spirit mediumship, religious rituals, spirituality

articles_hidden.title: Music-Based Interventions for  Cognition and Brain Health: the ARM framework
articles_hidden.authors: Psyche Loui; Jonathan E. Peelle; Jessica Adrienne Grahn
articles_hidden.abstract: Music-based interventions (MBIs) have shown promise in addressing cognitive, motor, and language impairments across neurological and neurodevelopmental conditions. Despite an increasing number of controlled studies that have assessed the potential rehabilitative effects of music, neural mechanisms underlying therapeutic benefits remain poorly understood. Here we present the ARM framework: a neurobiologically-informed model integrating three key systems: Auditory processing networks that encode temporal and spectral features; Reward circuitry activated by musical pleasure and prediction, and Motor systems engaged through auditory-motor coupling and rhythmic entrainment. We examine how specific MBIs leverage these systems to varying degrees and show how understanding these mechanisms is essential for predicting individual treatment response, personalizing interventions, and developing next-generation therapeutic approaches that optimize engagement of specific neural systems.

articles_hidden.title: Mentalizing across the Antagonism Spectrum: Opposing Associations with Callousness, Aggression, and Dishonesty
articles_hidden.authors: Michelle M. Berry; Scott D. Blain; Aisha Linnea Udochi; Muchen Xi; Colin G. DeYoung; Timothy Allen
articles_hidden.abstract: Theory of mind, or mentalizing, is the ability to infer what other people think and feel. Deficits in theory of mind are related to many of the interpersonal problems associated with antagonistic forms of psychopathology. Yet some antagonistic behaviors, such as deception, may benefit from accurately anticipating what another person believes. We tested whether three facets of antagonism – callousness, aggression, and dishonesty – showed opposing associations with mentalizing accuracy. Participants recruited online and from a university campus (N = 335) completed self-report measures of normal-range and pathological personality traits and three tasks that required them to reason about characters’ beliefs in stories, classify interactions between animated shapes, and identify mental states from photographs of the eyes. We used target-rotated exploratory structural equation modeling to estimate associations between the three antagonism facets and a latent factor capturing mentalizing across the tasks. Greater callousness and aggression were each associated with lower mentalizing accuracy, both when examined individually and when all three facets were modeled simultaneously. Greater dishonesty was associated with lower mentalizing accuracy when examined on its own, but with higher accuracy after accounting for callousness and aggression. Task-specific estimates generally followed the same directions but varied in magnitude and precision. These findings extend earlier single-task work and suggest that difficulty understanding others’ mental states may be more characteristic of some forms of antagonism than others.

articles_hidden.title: The Neural Basis of Consciousness During Evening Naps Measured by MEG: A Registered Report
articles_hidden.authors: Chikayo Hemmi; Angus Leung; Jennifer Windt; Yuki Motomura; Hiroshige Takeichi; Mochine Ishii; Takashi Tsutsumi; Yuri Kawabata; Naoko Takahashi; Shota Hosogai
articles_hidden.abstract: Dream experiences during sleep provide an excellent opportunity to investigate the neural basis of consciousness. Previous studies have examined the neural correlates of dreaming using electroencephalography (EEG), focusing on spectral power in specific frequency bands. However, findings have been inconsistent, particularly regarding the spatiotemporal characteristics of these correlates, raising questions about whether spectral power in specific brain regions and frequency bands reliably reflects dreaming. In this study, we investigate whether neural correlates reported in a highly influential EEG study generalize to consciousness during evening naps, measured using magnetoencephalography (MEG), which offers more accurate source reconstruction than EEG. In Stage 1, the data acquisition team completed data collection, obtaining MEG data and subjective reports using a targeted serial-awakening paradigm. We test the hypotheses that low-frequency neural power is lower, whereas high-frequency neural power is higher during conscious experiences in frontal and posterior regions. We defined data inclusion and exclusion criteria and established pre-specified analytical procedures based on data from two participants. The pilot results from one participant showed a tendency in the hypothesized direction for low-frequency power across regions, whereas no such tendency was observed for high-frequency power. The results from the other participant did not provide sufficient evidence for any of the hypotheses. In Stage 2, an independent analysis team will conduct group-level hypothesis testing according to the pre-specified procedure, using data from the remaining unanalyzed participants (N = 10) who meet the inclusion criteria.

articles_hidden.title: Examining associations between brain volume and alexithymia in autistic youth and young adults
