articles_hidden.authors: Goldie McQuaid; Gregory Wallace; Alex Job Said; Stefen Beeler-Duden; Zachary Jacokes; Kevin Pelphrey; Allison Jack
articles_hidden.abstract:
Alexithymia is a dimensional trait including challenges labeling emotions. Alexithymia is elevated in autistic individuals relative to the general population and is suggested to be part of the broader autism phenotype. Alexithymia is also independently associated with emotion regulation challenges, which are more prevalent among autistic persons, and with two of the most common co-occurring conditions among autistic people: depression and anxiety. A better understanding of alexithymia, including its neural correlates, therefore promises to advance our understanding of risk profiles for mental health problems in autistic people.

We therefore sought to: 1) characterize alexithymia in autistic (n=54) and neurotypical (n=56) adolescents and young adults (15-25y) including group and sex differences; 2) examine group and sex differences in brain volume in eight regions of interest implicated in alexithymia; and 3) explore potential interactions between group and brain volume as predictors of alexithymia.

Autistic individuals self-reported significantly higher levels of alexithymia relative to neurotypical individuals, with autistic females reporting the highest levels and neurotypical males the lowest levels. There were no differences in group or sex based on brain volume. Exploratory models predicting alexithymia found a significant interaction between group and right dorsal anterior cingulate cortex volume.

articles_hidden.title: Differences in associative change between cues trained in compound are better explained by individual prediction errors than by relative certainty
articles_hidden.authors: Amin Jahani; Metin Üngör
articles_hidden.abstract: The present experiments investigated associative changes during compound training involving cues with different learning histories. In six human predictive-learning experiments using the compound-test procedure (Rescorla, 2000), participants learned about the effects of foods (cues) on inflammation (outcome) in a hypothetical patient. Each food could cause decreases in inflammation, increases in inflammation, or had no effect. Cues A and C were trained as excitatory, whereas cues B and D were trained to acquire inhibitory properties. Participants then received compound training in which A and B were presented together and followed by an outcome that should produce associative loss, followed by a final test in which outcome expectations were assessed for the test compounds AD and BC. The initial training designs were expected to produce greater relative certainty about A than B, with A generating a larger individual prediction error than B during the compound training. If cues generating larger individual prediction errors undergo greater associative change, AD should receive lower ratings than BC. Alternatively, if participants preferentially attribute the compound outcome to the less certain cue (theory protection), BC should receive lower ratings than AD. Overall, the compound-test results were more consistent with an individual prediction-error account: AD was rated lower than BC in Experiments 1, 2, 5, and 6. Experiment 3 showed the opposite pattern, consistent with theory protection, but this pattern was not replicated in Experiment 4. We discuss the implications of these findings for the roles of prediction error and certainty in associative learning.

articles_hidden.title: A Dyadic Perspective on Reactive Aggression: Temporal Behavioral and Neural Dynamics in Sibling Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: Julia Koch; Lucia Hernandez-Pena; Dorothea M.G. König; Julia Schräder; Katja Bertsch; Andreas Meyer-Lindenberg; Edward S. Brodkin; Ute Habel; Rik Sijben; Lisa Wagels
articles_hidden.abstract: Aggression contributes to interpersonal conflict and societal harm. Although aggressive behavior unfolds within social interactions, it has largely been studied as an individual process. Siblings offer dyadic contexts in which aggression is shaped by developmental and relational dynamics. Here, we investigated how aggressive behavior and its neural correlates unfold dynamically within and across healthy adult siblings. Ninety-four siblings from 47 dyads completed an interactive version of the Taylor Aggression Paradigm (iTAP) during simultaneous functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI). We applied actor-partner interdependence models to predict each sibling’s neural activity during aggressive decision-making from both siblings’ neural responses during the preceding provocation feedback phase and tested whether these associations depended on relationship engagement, as measured by the Sibling Type Questionnaire (STQ) Mutuality subscale. Behaviorally, individuals’ subsequent responses were predicted by their own and their sibling’s preceding behavior. In parallel, greater ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) activity during provocation feedback was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity during aggressive decision-making within and across siblings, whereas lower dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (dmPFC) activity in one sibling was associated with greater subsequent amygdala activity in the other. Relationship engagement strengthened the actor vmPFC-amygdala association and moderated the partner vmPFC-amygdala association. Exploratory analyses linked dmPFC activity during provocation to participants’ previous aggressive decisions, but not subsequent aggression. Together, these findings show that aggression is embedded in temporally structured behavioral and neural dynamics involving both interaction partners, implicating medial prefrontal regulatory systems in dyadic interaction and highlighting the importance of interpersonal reciprocity and relationship history for understanding aggression.

articles_hidden.title: Born on Rhythms: Mother–Foetus and -Infant Neurophysiology as a Dynamic System of Metastable Coupled Oscillators
articles_hidden.authors: Anna Ciaunica; Earl K. Miller; Shir Atzil; Antonio Criscuolo
articles_hidden.abstract: The human embryo grows within a pulsatile maternal milieu structured by cardiac, respiratory, locomotor, vocal and circadian rhythms. Here we integrate evidence from embryology, foetal physiology, developmental cognitive neuroscience and chronobiology: we review how the foetal heart and placenta co-develop under maternal haemodynamic forcing, how maternal rhythms reach the foetus and how they may modulate foetal physiology. We propose that multimodal, semi-periodic input streams may provide a temporal reference frame scaffolding early timing abilities and autonomic self-regulation. In this view, we discuss that co-regulation may ground interoception and allostasis. Next, we formalize the mother–foetus and mother-infant dyads as multiscale systems of coupled oscillators spanning about seven orders of magnitude in frequency - from circadian cycles to neural oscillations. Within this coordination-dynamics framework we propose that healthy co-regulation is marked by metastability: flexible and transient coordination, preserving the endogenous tendencies for systems to display endogenous behaviours and to couple with other systems in an adaptive manner. The framework yields testable predictions on the link between dyadic coordination dynamics and developmental outcome. We are, quite literally, born on rhythms.

articles_hidden.title: Gender comes first: Experimental evidence for the representation of gender closer to the noun stem than number across linguistic populations
articles_hidden.authors: Carmen Saldana; Patrick Njue Kanampiu; Jennifer Culbertson
articles_hidden.abstract: Morphosyntactic expression exhibits significant cross-linguistic variation, yet systematic tendencies emerge. Gender and number features are frequently co-expressed within a single exponent, and when realised separately, gender morphology tends to surface closer to the stem. Competing theoretical accounts of gender and number seek to explain these tendencies, but empirical validation remains challenging due to sparse typological data. Across a series of artificial language learning experiments, we demonstrate that learners exhibit a robust preference for placing nominal morphology encoding gender information closest to the stem. This bias, consistent across English, Italian, and Kîîtharaka speakers, holds both for prefixing and suffixing morphology, and across different types of gender and number systems.These results provide a new source of empirical support for theories proposing a gender-first derivation and highlights cognitive constraints influencing morpheme order.

articles_hidden.title: Do Scales Semantically Resemble the Sources They Cite? Embedding Analysis of Construct Proliferation in Five Anomy Instruments
articles_hidden.authors: Mateo Belalcazar; Joan Sebastian Diaz Mona; Nelson Molina Valencia; Yenny Otálora
articles_hidden.abstract:
Construct proliferation in psychology is associated with jingle and jangle fallacies that psychometric methods are not designed to detect. Semantic embeddings offer a complementary approach, but existing applications have compared scales within a single level without bringing in the theoretical texts a construct's tradition rests on. This study extends the embedding framework of Wulff and Mata (2025a) to a
cross-level comparison paired with a documentary audit of citation acts. We embedded 43 items from five anomy scales alongside 3,762 propositions extracted from nine source texts at three analytical levels (foundational texts, scale articles, and items), using six embedding models from three architectural families, and we coded every passage in which a scale article cites a theoretical source. Items formed
  thematic clusters that crossed scale boundaries, beyond the expression of a single homogeneous theme per instrument, while retaining within-scale cohesion, and were rarely nearest to the article that introduced them (14%). All five scale articles were semantically nearest to Merton's (1938) text, a pattern identical across models, stable under bootstrap resampling, and not reproduced by two genre-matched control texts. The documentary audit showed that no article adopts Merton's formulation; the two articles that adopt a foundational text both adopt Durkheim's Suicide, which was the nearest foundation for neither of them. This proximity coexists with the absence of any direct adoption of Merton. This extension, combining semantic proximity with documented citation acts, offers an approach for examining whether the sources an instrument cites are also the ones its content most resembles.

articles_hidden.title: Motivational Framing Shapes Effort Judgments in Individuals with Depressive Symptoms
articles_hidden.authors: Thomas Meyer; Rebecca Kochtokrax; Hannah Sautmann; Nexhmedin Morina
articles_hidden.abstract: Effort-related motivational deficits in depression are often studied through effort-reward decisions, yet everyday effort also depends on the reference standards against which it is judged. In a preregistered laboratory crossover study, 51 participants with at least mild depressive symptoms received two opposing effort framings: self-initiated allocation toward goals and need frustration emphasizing burden and affective demand. After reconstructing previous-day activities, participants evaluated upward and downward social, temporal-past, criteria-based, and counterfactual standards for their two most effortful activities per session, yielding 1,632 standard-endorsement judgments followed by intensity and discrepancy ratings for endorsed standards. As predicted, need-frustration framing increased endorsement of upward criteria-based standards (“this should feel less effortful”). However, this effect did not generalize across upward comparisons. Instead, need frustration decreased upward temporal standards (“this used to feel easier”) and increased downward counterfactual standards (“it could have been harder under worse circumstances”). Intensity ratings among endorsed standards were not reliably affected, although an exploratory relevance score supported the specific role of upward criteria-based standards. Perceived effort was higher under allocation but correlated more positively with depressive symptoms under need frustration. These findings suggest that motivational framing changes the comparison standards people identify as relevant to everyday effort judgments and highlight the need to assess the appraised meaning of effort-related comparisons directly.

articles_hidden.title: Researching Traditionally Rooted Psychological Concepts: Methodological Implications from Traditional Chinese Psychology
articles_hidden.authors: Xianglong ZENG
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on psychological concepts rooted in historical intellectual traditions has attracted growing attention, yet studies in this field may investigate fundamentally different psychological objects. The present article conceptualizes the modern and traditional approaches to such research and systematically examines their methodological implications. Whereas the modern approach constitutes its objects primarily through contemporary manifestations within a population, the traditional approach specifies psychological targets through theoretical formulations grounded in classical accounts. Such targets may have theoretically specified internal relations and need not already be realized in the populations available for research. Drawing on existing studies of traditional Chinese psychology, the analysis identifies potential methodological mismatches and demonstrates their implications for empirical investigation. Ordinary participants may not possess the understanding or degree of realization required to investigate a target mentality; cultivation may be a methodological precondition rather than merely an intervention to modify existing tendencies; and satisfactory psychometric results do not necessarily establish that a measure represents the target’s intended meanings and internal relations. Moreover, findings from partial realizations cannot simply be generalized to fully cultivated forms. These analyses provide principles for selecting participants, determining the role of intervention, evaluating measurement, and delimiting the scope of inference according to the intended research object and question. The article also considers how empirical evidence can inform the evaluation and possible revision of classical psychological claims, while distinguishing empirical investigation from the normative justification of cultivation. Beyond traditional psychology, these methodological insights may inform empirical research on psychological possibilities specified through other theoretical sources.

articles_hidden.title: Language at Scale: Functional Informational Interchangeability and the Child–LLM Data Gap
articles_hidden.authors: Yonata Levy
articles_hidden.abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) achieve remarkable linguistic competence through exposure to
far more language than children ever encounter. We examine whether this Child–LLM data gap
rests on an incomplete comparison of the information available to children. Drawing on language
acquisition research and information theory, we propose Functional Informational
Interchangeability: extensive linguistic input can supply models with information that is
interchangeable with the information children obtain through combined linguistic, perceptual,
motor, emotional and social experiences. Relevance, redundancy, joint information and learnerdependent uptake provide tools for testing this hypothesis. The proposal reframes the Child–
LLM data gap around information relevant to acquiring linguistic knowledge. If the
contributions of these environments prove comparable in task-relevant informational units, the
apparent gap may disappear.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable prospective effects between workplace incivility and depressive and anxious mood: A reassessment of Cao et al. (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles_hidden.abstract: Cao et al. reported longitudinal associations between workplace incivility and depressive and anxious mood based on cross-lagged panel analyses. However, the detection of statistically significant cross-lagged coefficients does not necessarily demonstrate the existence of underlying prospective effects because comparable patterns can emerge under alternative data-generating mechanisms. In the present study, we recreated the sample size and correlational structure reported by Cao et al. using simulated data and evaluated the robustness of the findings across several analytically defensible model specifications. The estimated effects varied markedly across approaches. Whereas some models yielded positive prospective associations, others produced negative or statistically nonsignificant estimates. When the results from all specifications were synthesized using meta-analytic techniques, none of the aggregated effects differed significantly from zero. These findings suggest that available evidence does not provide a strong basis for claims about prospective relationships between workplace incivility and depressive or anxious mood. In line with recommendations from the multiverse-analysis literature, inferences should be guided by the extent to which results replicate across reasonable analytical decisions rather than by a single modeling strategy.

articles_hidden.title: “Huge if true”: Aspirational believing and the appeal of conspiracy theories
articles_hidden.authors: Sander Van de Cruys
articles_hidden.abstract:
Why do people believe in conspiracy theories? I propose that part of the answer lies in what our metacognitive feelings track. Curiosity and the aha experience are fallible markers of truth, but good markers of subjective progress: of gaining grip on a problem through one’s own inquiry. This leads to a different view of belief, which I call aspirational believing. People may accept hypotheses on thinner evidence when acting on them promises control, because that action opens new channels for evidence and agency, whether or not the hypothesis is true. In moderation this sustains exploration, but pushed too far, belief stops reacting to evidence. Conspiracy theories are a prime example of this. They turn diffuse, uncontrollable experiences into plots that can be probed and exposed, and their “do
your own research” arcs reliably deliver the felt insights that signal progress. The approach does not require that conspiracy believers experience an unusual need for certainty or control, just that they are optimistically biased in their control expectations (like most of us). I distinguish this account from motivated reasoning, error management and compensatory control accounts, and derive diverging, testable predictions. I close with a tentative remedy: fostering (epistemic and pragmatic) agency may matter more than cleaning up information diets.

articles_hidden.title: The cognitive and social origins of randomization devices
articles_hidden.authors: Tal Boger; Dorsa Amir
articles_hidden.abstract: From throwing dice to reading tea leaves, humans across diverse cultures, eras, and geographies rely on decision aids that produce randomness. What purpose do these aids serve, and why do cultures create them with such regularity? In this Perspective, we unify these seemingly disparate tools as randomization devices, and argue that they culturally evolved to solve two recurrent problems, one cognitive and one social. Specifically, randomization devices produce strong, unpredictable randomness, whereas human cognition does not; and randomization devices externalize decisions in ways that create a social buffer between decision-makers and outcomes. The design of such devices reflects these constraints, even in relation to unique mechanistic features. We focus on one such property — causal opacity — as an important feature of randomization devices that subserves their function and arises in diverse literatures spanning cultural evolution, computer science, and political philosophy. Taken together, we argue that the widespread recurrence of randomization devices reflects widespread cognitive constraints and social demands.

articles_hidden.title: Distinguishing ingroup and outgroup germ aversion improves prediction of intergroup attitudes during the COVID-19 pandemic
articles_hidden.authors: Jeana Kataria; Brian O'Shea
articles_hidden.abstract: During infectious disease outbreaks, contamination concerns can become attached to social groups. Existing germ-aversion measures rarely specify the perceived source of contamination. Using data collected during the first U.S. peak of COVID-19, we tested whether target-specific germ aversion (ingroups/local region versus outgroups/developing countries) improves the prediction of intergroup attitudes during the COVID-19 pandemic, reflecting the possibility that unfamiliar outgroups are perceived as greater sources of novel pathogens. Across explicit (e.g., perceived health and warmth; Ns = 1,450–1,460) and implicit (Brief Implicit Association Test; Ns = 378–1,311) attitudes targeting ingroups (US, White People) and outgroups (China, Italy, UK, Asian, Brown and Black People), we find that outgroup—but not ingroup or general—germ aversion was the most consistent predictor of ingroup preference and outgroup derogation, even after controlling for infectability and COVID-19 concern. These results suggest that contamination concerns linked to foreign or developing-country contexts can provide modest incremental information about intergroup attitudes during a politicised public-health crisis, highlighting the value of specifying the targets and contexts of pathogen concern when applying disease-avoidance psychology to intergroup questions.

articles_hidden.title: The role of neuroscience for psychological causal explanation
articles_hidden.authors: Beate Krickel; Markus Werkle-Bergner
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology provides causal explanations of behavior but it remains contested whether such explanations are scientifically legitimate without grounding in neuroscience. Two prominent arguments have been put forward to argue for the dependence of psychology on neuroscience: first, the classical causal exclusion argument argues that higher-level causes are excluded by lower-level causes. Second, according to a more recent argument, psychological models only provide how-possibly explanations but not how-actually explanations unless the variables and relations they postulate correspond to underlying neural mechanisms. In this article, we defend the independence of psychological causal explanation. Based on an interventionist account of causation, we argue that a psychological model is causally explanatory when it identifies variables that serve as points of intervention. Still, we show that neuroscience sometimes has a crucial role for validating psychological models: when a psychological model identifies points of interventions that cannot be intervened on at the psychological level.

articles_hidden.title: Dynamic resource allocation in temporal working memory: interplay of decay, interference and attention
articles_hidden.authors: Yunyun Shen; Sophie K Herbst; Virginie van Wassenhove
articles_hidden.abstract: How does a moment become a memory trace? The transition from perceived duration to the when of memory is likely shaped by attention and working memory (WM). In two experiments, we investigated how memory decay, interference between stored durations, and internal versus external attention affect the precision of recall from temporal WM. For this, we used a delayed reproduction task in which participants listened to a sequence of time intervals and reproduced them after a retention period (Herbst et al., 2025). In Experiment 1, we manipulated the ratio between the target interval and the retention interval, showing that both the duration of the retention interval (decay) and its ratio to the target (temporal distinctiveness yielding interference) affected WM performance. In Experiment 2, we examined interference between intervals within a sequence by manipulating attention via a cue indicating which interval to reproduce. The cue appeared either before (pro-cue) or after (retro-cue) the retention period, directing external attention to sensory encoding or internal attention to WM representations, respectively, either for a single item or the full sequence. External attention selectively benefited accuracy and precision for the longest item when cued alone in the final position. Retro-cueing, by contrast, more generally reduced precision for single-item compared to the whole-sequence recall. Finally, a mixture modeling approach revealed swap errors consistent with those observed in visual WM. Together, these findings compare the contributions of decay and temporal distinctiveness to temporal WM performance with a dynamic resource allocation framework.

articles_hidden.title: Establishing the Observant Attention Trait
articles_hidden.authors: Chris Robert Harrison Brown; Vlad Costin; Sophie Forster
articles_hidden.abstract: The characteristic of being observant is a widely acknowledged socio-cultural phenomenon, referring to an individuals’ tendency to be aware of their surrounding environment. However, perhaps due to the lack of a suitable measure, this trait is not yet empirically evidenced or theoretically recognized. Here we sought to empirically establish the construct of an ‘Observant Attention trait’. We developed a novel 19-item self-report measure across multiple large samples (total responses N = 2,441 predominantly undergraduate students). This measure revealed an underlying ‘Observant Attention’ (OA) factor across three sub-factors; specifically, the awareness of subtle details and changes (‘Noticing awareness’), awareness of unexpected motivationally relevant stimuli (‘Alerting awareness’), and awareness of olfactory stimuli (‘Olfactory awareness’). The factor structure and reliability of this model was consistent across multiple samples and confirmed in a pre-registered replication. Test-retest analysis indicated that OA scores remained stable even after a year-long interval. OA showed either no relation to or weak correlations with existing attentional traits, suggesting that it is not adequately indexed by these existing measures, and was also moderately related to patterns of neurodiversity and social distancing failures. OA was only weakly linked to inattentional blindness, consistent with a view that single noticing events may be primarily determined by situational influences, but trait influences may emerge across the countless noticing opportunities that arise within any given day. The current investigation hence provides initial empirical evidence to support the theoretical construct of an Observant Attention Trait, and introduces a reliable measure that enables further study of this trait.

articles_hidden.title: Math Ability Rating Questionnaire (MARQ) for Adults:  Validating a New Self-report Measure
articles_hidden.authors: Daria Khanolainen; Elsje van Bergen; Asko Tolvanen; Tuire Koponen; Jenni Salminen; Minna Torppa; Britt Min; Madelief Isabel Kuijper
articles_hidden.abstract:
From a clinical perspective, identifying individuals with mathematical difficulties is essential for offering support. However, these individuals often avoid mathematical tests due to co-occurring mathematical anxiety. From a research perspective, this leads to systematic data missingness. Moreover, in large-scale research, direct testing is often not feasible because of time and resource constraints. Here, we develop a self-report scale for screening for mathematical difficulties in adults as a cost-effective and time-efficient alternative to mathematical tests. Our mathematical ability rating questionnaire (MARQ) is available in full (19 items) and brief (3 items) versions. The MARQ was developed using a sample of 278 Finnish adults. Participants completed four mathematical tests and filled out a 30-item questionnaire, developed based on extensive literature review. Regression analysis, item response theory, and confirmatory factor analysis were used to identify the items most strongly associated with directly assessed mathematical skills. The full and brief versions of the MARQ had good internal consistency (α = 0.94 and 0.86, respectively) and correlated with mathematical skills (−0.70 and −0.63), mathematical anxiety (0.72 and 0.69), mathematical enjoyment (−0.58 and 0.50), and their children’s mathematical skills (−0.24 and −0.22). The full MARQ accurately identified 93% of adults with higher mathematical skills (test scores above −1 SD) and 52% with lower skills (test scores below −1 SD). A preliminary Dutch replication among university students demonstrated strong internal consistency (α = .86) of the full MARQ but weaker associations with arithmetic fluency (−.23). Overall, the findings support the MARQ as a reliable and scalable tool for assessing self-perceived mathematical ability, particularly in Finnish-speaking populations.
CITE: Khanolainen, D., van Bergen, E., Tolvanen, A., Min, B., Kuijper, M. I., Koponen, T., Salminen, J., & Torppa, M. (in press). Mathematical ability rating questionnaire (MARQ) for adults: Validating a new self-report measure. Journal of Numerical Cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Social prioritization of others can be explained by representational  closeness to the self
articles_hidden.authors: Meike Scheller; Georgios Velimachitis; Gabrielle Foster; Greesha Yadav
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual cognition is shaped not only by sensory input, but also by social relevance. While self-related information is processed preferentially, similar advantages extend to close others. How prioritization rapidly extends to others, however, remains unclear. We propose a framework of ‘representational closeness’, whereby individuals cognitively represented closer to the self, benefit from more efficient processing. Devising three markers – closeness, boundary imprecision, overlap – in a reanalysis of Scheller & Sui (2022, n = 43) and a new experiment (n = 78), we show that this framework explains processing benefits across two domains: friends over strangers, and more over less attractive strangers. Faster and more accurate responses, reduced response variability, and increased self-other confusion tracked representational closeness. These findings suggest that prioritization reflects a general organising principle of social perception through which cognitive resources are dynamically allocated according to social relevance, linking visual processing to the structure of social representation.

articles_hidden.title: A clinician-informed framework for precision psychotherapy in psychosis
articles_hidden.authors: Shenaya Maria Lisboa; Maria Chiara Del Piccolo; Inês Eulálio; Anna Georgiades; Sandra Vieira
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) is the recommended psychosocial intervention for early psychosis;
however, treatment response remains heterogeneous. Precision psychotherapy aims to personalise
treatment by identifying individual characteristics that may predict differential treatment response and
inform treatment selection. However, most precision psychotherapy studies rely on retrospective data
collected using assessment protocols not designed to identify predictors of treatment response and may
therefore fail to capture the full range of characteristics relevant to treatment personalisation. We aimed to
review and expand the current set of predictors used in the literature in CBT from the perspective of
clinicians. Methods. Twenty Clinical Psychologists participated in semi-structured interviews. Clinician-informed predictors were
identified through inductive analysis of unprompted accounts. Clinicians subsequently rated the perceived
importance of these and 32 literature-derived factors on a 10-point scale. Mean ratings and variability were
examined to characterise clinician agreement. Findings were integrated into a candidate predictor
framework linked to available measurement instruments. Results. Clinicians spontaneously identified 38 factors, of which 16 were absent from the literature-derived list.
Factors considered important for engagement with, and benefit from CBTp included cognitive processes,
symptom characteristics, illness history, psychosocial functioning, and migrant status. Clinicians also
identified several under-investigated therapy-related and clinical factors, such as expectations and
understanding of therapy, readiness and motivation for treatment, medication use, level of risk, and
substance misuse. Demographic characteristics more broadly, and basic neurocognitive performance, were
generally considered less important. Conclusion. The resulting clinician-informed framework provides a broader, clinically grounded set of candidate
predictors to inform prospective research into personalised CBTp.

articles_hidden.title: The State of Play: Methodological Reflections on Phenomenological Psychopathology
articles_hidden.authors: Jodie Louise Russell; Lucienne Spencer; Matthew Broome
articles_hidden.abstract: In this paper, we reflect on the position of the researcher within the field of phenomenological psychopathology and the ways they can overcome privilege and outsider status in order to more accurately and ethically grasp the structure of disorder experience from the perspective of the person living it. §1 discusses problems incorporating lived experience as well as its challenges within phenomenological psychopathology. §2 introduces the phenomenological notion of play in the work of Husserl and Fink. §3 elaborates on the political and ethical dimensions of play using the work of Lugones, and §4 then discusses how playfulness might be applied in health research to overcome the problems outlined in §1. §5 then gives examples of how play might be utilised within the methodology of phenomenological psychopathology. Overall, we suggest that both researchers and those with lived experience can engage in processes of understanding that can facilitate safe and inclusive interactions through the medium of play.

articles_hidden.title: Cognitive variability on stable ground:  A narrative review of cognitive fluctuation in childhood and adolescence and hands-on tutorial in quantifying (cognitive) variability
articles_hidden.authors: Jordy van Langen; Michael Aristodemou; Rogier Kievit
articles_hidden.abstract: The importance of cognitive variability in development has been discussed for over a century, but empirical work has lagged behind. However, recent technological and methodological advances have led to a substantial increase in studies focused on cognitive variability in developmental populations. Here we review recent empirical work on cognitive variability during development, examining the cognitive and neural mechanisms underlying individual differences and developmental changes in cognitive variability. We synthesize empirical evidence to show that cognitive variability: (1) decreases with expertise and age during development; (2) carries unique information about cognition above and beyond mean performance; (3) is observed across a wide range of cognitive domains, with more domain-specific sources of variation than those underlying mean performance; (4) is a developmentally relevant correlate of neurodevelopmental disorders; (5) can be either adaptive or maladaptive depending on the context; and (6) can be modified through behavioral and pharmacological interventions. We discuss variations in methods and tasks to quantify cognitive variability, and provide a hands-on tutorial for applied researchers to estimate different measures of (cognitive) variability for trial level data to guide current and future work on cognitive variability.

articles_hidden.title: Hierarchical knowledge and skills undermine payoff-biased social learning
articles_hidden.authors: Nanda Ramo Jafarian; Björn Lindström; Ingmar Visser; Annemie Ploeger; Pieter van den Berg; Lucas Molleman
articles_hidden.abstract: Acquiring skills and knowledge (“traits”) through social learning is central to human development and cultural evolution. Yet it remains unclear how individuals can effectively learn from others when traits form hierarchies, with advanced traits building on more basic ones. We present a model showing that trait hierarchies favour “proximal social learning” where individuals copy others who are only slightly more knowledgeable. In contrast, payoff bias - often assumed to be universally advantageous - performs poorly because it directs learners toward advanced traits they lack the basics for. Our experiments demonstrate that people indeed shift to proximal social learning when conditions favour it. Our results challenge core assumptions of mainstream cultural evolution theory and highlight that trait hierarchies are a key factor shaping human social learning.

articles_hidden.title: Detecting Response Styles in Visual Analogue Scales
articles_hidden.authors: Dominik Vollbracht; Tanja Lischetzke; Mirka Henninger
articles_hidden.abstract: Response styles are prevalent in self-report data and may bias parameter estimates. While there are various approaches for detecting response styles in Likert-type data, models for visual analogue scales remain scarce. We propose a novel modeling framework that extends the beta item response model by Noel and Dauvier (2007) to jointly detect extreme response style, midpoint response style, and acquiescent response style. Estimated in a Bayesian framework using Stan, the model performed well in a comprehensive simulation study. Parameter recovery was primarily influenced by the number of (reverse-scored) items and the variance of response styles, whereas sample size had a negligible effect. The model’s practical utility is illustrated using empirical data (Kuhlmann et al., 2017), for which it demonstrated superior model fit compared to the original beta item response model. Overall, the proposed framework provides researchers with a principled approach to account for response styles in visual analogue scale data.

articles_hidden.title: The Social Consequences of Ability Grouping in Schools
articles_hidden.authors: Maud Nijland; Jellie Sierksma
articles_hidden.abstract: Schools worldwide sort children into ability groups to improve achievement. Little research has tested how this practice changes children’s social lives. Psychological research shows, however, that group distinctions shape social interactions. This preregistered study asks: What are the social consequences of ability grouping in secondary school? We showed Dutch 10-to-18-year-olds (N = 332, 97.3% native Dutch, 51.2% boys, 47.6% girls, 1.2% other, collected in 2025) peers who performed well, intermediately, and less well at school and manipulated, between subjects, whether performance levels came with an ability group label. Without group labels, achievement had no effect on how adolescents in low and intermediate groups felt about peers. With group labels, adolescents in low-ability groups felt less close to high-ability groups and were less willing to meet up to peers in high- and intermediate-ability groups; adolescents in intermediate-ability groups felt less close to peers in low-ability groups. Adolescents in high-ability groups always preferred higher-achieving peers, regardless of group labels. Salient labels also made adolescents defend a school system with ability grouping more, whereas third-party friendship predictions were unaffected. Our research suggests that ability grouping fosters social segregation and leads adolescents to see the system that produces this segregation as more legitimate.

articles_hidden.title: Momentary Emotion Differentiation:  A Theory-Consistent Index that is Disambiguated from Momentary Affect
articles_hidden.authors: Yiqin Zhu; Matthew H. S. Ng; Richard Morris; Renee J Thompson
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotion differentiation (ED), the ability to distinguish among one’s emotional experiences, has been increasingly studied as a momentary process. Extending ED measurement in this way raises questions about what a momentary ED index should capture and how it should relate to momentary affect and perceived sources of emotion. We derived a divergence-based index and compared it with an existing sum-based ED index in two ecological momentary assessment (EMA) studies. College students (Sample 1; N = 268) and community adults (Sample 2; N = 179) reported emotions five times a day for 12 or 14 days, respectively. Individuals in Sample 1 also reported perceived source and fit of emotions. Divergence-based ED captures how emotion ratings depart from one another, while sum-based ED captures shared shifts across ratings. Across samples, both indices, when aggregated, yielded the same rank ordering as trait-level ED, and showed substantial within-person fluctuations. Divergence-based ED retained most of its within-person variance after adjusting for momentary affect or squared affect, while sum-based ED retained little after adjusting for squared affect. In Sample 1, greater-than-usual clarity about the source of feelings and better-than-usual fit between feelings and the situations were associated with higher divergence-based ED and lower sum-based ED. Simulations identified conditions under which response-scale endpoints can produce artifactual associations between divergence-based ED and momentary affect. Findings support appropriate use of divergence-based ED, especially as an outcome when momentary affect needs to be considered. We provide design and analysis recommendations and R code for applying divergence-based ED to EMA datasets.

articles_hidden.title: Cross-Cultural Adaptation of the Life in Recovery Survey: Recovery Concepts and Pathways in the Spanish Context
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Serrano-Pastor; Alfredo Zarco Alpuente; Paula Samper-Garcia; David Alcaina-Serrano; Guillermo Blanco-Bailac; María Teresa Bobes-Bascaran; María Jesús Flores-Fresco; Francisco Javier García-Hernández; Begoña Gómez-Monfort; Pedro Gómez-Linares
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: The Life in Recovery (LiR) survey has been used internationally to examine addiction recovery, but little is known about how its concepts and content transfer across sociocultural and service contexts. This study culturally adapted the LiR survey for use in Spain and examined evidence based on test content and response processes.
Methods: A sequential mixed-methods process included review of previous LiR versions, translation, contextual adaptation, expert review (N = 13), and cognitive interviews with people in recovery (N = 6). Expert agreement was examined using Item-level Content Validity Indexes (I-CVI), and qualitative data were analysed using framework analysis.
Results: Twenty-five of 37 survey questions met the predefined I-CVI criterion, while most items met criteria for clarity (76/80) and relevance (60/80). Expert review and cognitive interviews led to substantial conceptual, linguistic, and contextual modifications: contextual information was expanded and repositioned; recovery questions were reformulated to better capture recovery onset, relapse, and self-identified recovery stage, incorporating the non-linear nature of recovery; recovery pathways were adapted to the Spanish addiction care system; and the SABRS was reduced from 32 to 24 items while retaining its core domains and facilitating cross-cultural comparability.
Conclusions: Cross-cultural adaptation of the LiR required changes beyond linguistic translation to reflect local recovery meanings, lived experiences, and the Spanish addiction-care system. The findings illustrate the importance of balancing international comparability with cultural and contextual relevance when adapting recovery measures across settings.

articles_hidden.title: What Do Global Life Evaluations Capture?
articles_hidden.authors: Irene Johanna Elisabeth Teulings; Espen Røysamb; Ludvig Daae Bjørndal; Esten Høyland Leonardsen; Ragnhild Bang Nes; Jinrui Liu; Matthew Iasiello; Joar Vittersø
articles_hidden.abstract: Life satisfaction is widely used as a primary indicator of population wellbeing in research and policymaking. Yet it remains unclear which wellbeing domains contribute to life satisfaction and other global life evaluations. In a UK sample (N = 1,050), we examined how four global measures (Satisfaction With Life Scale, single-item life satisfaction, Cantril’s Ladder, a good life evaluation) reflected experiences across 15 wellbeing domains. Machine learning analyses identified optimism, personal circumstances, happiness, and meaning and purpose as the strongest predictors, with other domains contributing little predictive information. Crucially, domains’ contributions corresponded only weakly with participants’ domain importance ratings, challenging the assumption that unequal contributions of domains reflect what people value most. Global life evaluations thus appear to provide selectively weighted rather than comprehensive summaries of wellbeing, potentially underrepresenting certain domains people consider important. Researchers and policymakers seeking comprehensive or value-based assessments could therefore complement global measures with multidimensional assessments.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Diagnostic Categories: Policy Implications of Dimensional Classification of Mental Disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Aidan G.C. Wright; Christopher James Hopwood
articles_hidden.abstract: Debates about whether psychiatric classification of mental illness should shift from the current categories (i.e., you have a diagnosis or you do not) to dimensions (i.e., people all fall along a spectrum of severity) has intensified in recent years. The balance of evidence strongly favors dimensional models, and official diagnostic manuals are considering widespread adoption of dimensional systems for diagnosis. We consider what follows for policies that interface with mental health, drawing primarily on United States examples. Policies across law, insurance, disability, drug regulation, licensing, and education already combine diagnostic categories with eligibility standards defined by the relevant organizations. Dimensional classification systems will make the distinction between clinical description and policy driven decision rules more explicit. We argue that mental health symptoms and functional impairment should be assessed separately, and that policies should turn on evidence relevant to treatment need, daily functioning, and risk. We offer seven recommendations for developing, evaluating, and implementing such standards. Explicit thresholds of functioning for context-relevant impairment could improve policy without making a diagnostic label or numerical score the sole basis for granting services or restricting rights.

articles_hidden.title: Mitigating Retest Effects in High-Frequency Cognitive Assessment Data: A Tutorial on the Bayesian Double Exponential Model in Stan
articles_hidden.authors: Yanling Li; Joachim Vandekerckhove; Grace J. Chen; Martin Sliwinski; Zita Oravecz
articles_hidden.abstract: In this tutorial, we give a comprehensive, step-by-step guide for implementing the Bayesian Double Exponential Model (BDEM) in the popular Bayesian software Stan. The BDEM is a statistical tool designed to disentangle retest effects from true longitudinal cognitive change and to quantify individual differences in high-frequency repeated cognitive assessment data, typically collected in everyday settings. We give step-by-step guidelines for fitting BDEM in Stan and also describe implementations in PyMC and JAGS in an online supplement. Finally, we provide a real data example to highlight the unique inferences that can be drawn with our approach. The goal of this tutorial is to equip researchers with the necessary tools to apply advanced multilevel models of cognitive change and retest learning in high-frequency assessment designs.

articles_hidden.title: Short-Term Efficiency, Long-Term Cognitive Cost? A Systematic Literature Review of Large Language Model Use in Professional Work
articles_hidden.authors: Chetna Khandare
articles_hidden.abstract:
Many professionals now use large language models (LLMs) at work, and experiments show that the tools make many tasks
faster and improve the immediate output. The worry is that these gains may cost workers some of the skill, judgement and self-knowledge
they would otherwise build or keep. We systematically reviewed empirical research on the cognitive and performance consequences of
LLM use among workers and professionals, published between January 2020 and November 2026. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines,
we identified 1,559 records in OpenAlex and Europe PMC and five further studies through citation searching. After screening, 157 studies
remained. Two-thirds were published in 2026, and most come from software development, healthcare and general knowledge work.
Randomised and field experiments consistently report short-term gains in speed, output and quality, typically largest for less experienced
workers. These gains are task-dependent, and LLM-assisted professionals frequently fail to match the model working alone. Fewer than ten
studies measured unaided performance, memory or skill after LLM use. Those that did reported reduced recall of AI-assisted work,
impaired skill formation and fragility when access was disrupted. Cross-sectional studies link reliance and confidence in AI with lower
self-reported critical thinking and professional self-efficacy, but self-reported capability loss did not track objective performance.
Experience, task fit, mode of use, AI literacy and verification behaviour emerged as moderators. We conclude that the short-term efficiency
gain is well supported, while the long-term cognitive cost remains plausible but largely untested in professional settings. We propose a
framework and research agenda centred on longitudinal and withdrawal-based designs.

articles_hidden.title: Inference-Time Self-Guidance for Conversational Safety in Delusion-Related Interactions
articles_hidden.authors: David Piterman; Elad Refoua; Hadar Dery; Gunther Meinlschmidt; Ziv Ben-Zion; Kfir Bar; Zohar Elyoseph
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in psychologically sensitive conversations, where repeated affirmation may reinforce delusion-related beliefs and associated risk. Inference-time self-guidance, in which a model generates conversation-specific guidance for subsequent responses without parameter updates, may offer an approach to conversational safety, but its utility in delusion-related interactions remains unclear.
Objective: To develop and evaluate conversation-specific inference-time self-guidance for conversational safety in delusion-related interactions.
Methods: In this preregistered study, Gemini 2.5 Pro, GPT-5, and DeepSeek V4 Flash completed 16 Psychosis-Bench scenarios under Baseline and three self-guidance conditions: response rules, contrastive examples, and short-horizon consequence simulation. The fully crossed design yielded 192 conversations and 2,304 assistant turns. A separate automated judge scored Delusion Confirmation (DCS), Harm Enablement (HES), and Safety Intervention (SIS) using published Psychosis-Bench rubrics. Analyses compared benchmark-defined Explicit and Implicit risk-cue scenarios and examined whether self-guidance reduced this gap.
Results: Across models, all three self-guidance conditions significantly reduced delusion confirmation and harm enablement and increased safety intervention relative to Baseline (all nine PFDR<.001; dz = 1.10–2.17). At Baseline, explicit risk cues elicited significantly greater SIS than matched implicit cues, whereas cue-type differences in DCS and HES were not significant. Self-guidance did not significantly attenuate the explicit–implicit safety gap after correction for multiple comparisons.
Conclusions: Model-generated inference-time self-guidance improved benchmark-defined safety behavior during standardized scripted escalation without parameter updates. These findings support further evaluation of inference-time self-guidance for delusion-related conversational safety, particularly when risk is communicated indirectly.

articles_hidden.title: Attentional Bias as an Intermediate Mechanism Linking Executive Dysfunction to Emotional Dysregulation in ADHD
articles_hidden.authors: Mahdieh Vaezbarenji; Edmund Sonuga-Barke
articles_hidden.abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is increasingly recognised as involving persistent difficulties in emotion regulation alongside well-established executive dysfunction. However, the cognitive mechanisms linking executive control impairments to emotional dysregulation remain insufficiently integrated within existing theoretical models. The present conceptual review proposes that attentional bias toward emotionally salient stimuli represents an intermediate cognitive-affective mechanism linking executive dysfunction to emotional dysregulation in ADHD. Drawing on evidence from attentional processing, executive control, affective neuroscience, and neurobiological models of ADHD, the review argues that impaired top-down prefrontal regulatory systems reduce the ability to suppress stimulus-driven attentional capture by emotionally salient information. Consequently, biased attentional allocation may amplify emotional reactivity, prolong engagement with negative affective stimuli, and interfere with adaptive emotion regulation processes. Neurobiologically, disrupted functional connectivity between prefrontal regulatory networks and salience-processing systems, including the amygdala, anterior cingulate cortex, and ventral striatum, may contribute to both attentional and emotional dysregulation in ADHD. The review further discusses theoretical and clinical implications of this framework, including the potential value of interventions targeting attentional control and emotional attentional processing. Limitations of the current evidence base and directions for future longitudinal and neurobiological research are also considered. Conceptualising attentional bias within a broader neurocognitive framework may provide a more integrated and mechanistically coherent account of emotional dysregulation in ADHD.

articles_hidden.title: Neural representational changes after category learning across sensory modalities: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Anthony Cruz; Madeline Bloomberg; John Paul Minda
articles_hidden.abstract: Category learning is a fundamental mechanism underlying concept formation, yet the extent to which it induces stable neural representational changes across sensory modalities remains unclear. This preregistered systematic review assesses functional neuroimaging studies that examined whether experience with a novel category structure alters the brain’s responses to the newly categorized stimuli, specifically outside of active categorization. Across 26 experiments meeting inclusion criteria, 81% reported learning-related changes in neural representations of stimuli following category acquisition. These effects were observed using fMRI, EEG, and MEG in a variety of paradigms. Eighteen visual and seven auditory studies tended to find these changes in higher-order cortical regions associated with object and speech processing. Other kinds of evidence were sparse. The single olfactory study found altered patterns of connectivity following learning. A minority of studies (5/26) found no evidence of task-independent representational changes, with task-dependent or null results being reported. The current state of the literature suggests that category learning can produce durable changes in the neural representations of stimuli in the brain, with the loci and nature of these changes varying across modalities. Limitations of the existing literature and suggestions for future work are highlighted.

articles_hidden.title: Decoding Affect: A Computational Model of Affective Adaptation and Construction
articles_hidden.authors: Haijiao Cui; Liu-Fang Zhou
articles_hidden.abstract: Affective construction and adaptation are complementary processes through which affective value is generated and evolves over time. Although prior research has identified key determinants of these processes, including reference points, stimulus inherent value, attention, negativity bias, adaptation rate, and time, a unified framework that quantifies how these factors interact and jointly shape affect remains lacking, leaving important nonlinear affective phenomena insufficiently explained. We propose the Attention-Reference Interaction Adaptation (ARIA) framework, which formalizes affective valuation as an attention-gated dual-reference integration process that evaluates current sensory inputs relative to both prior experience and allostatic set-points. By specifying how value salience and negativity bias jointly govern attention allocation and adaptation rate, ARIA suggests that relativity and asymmetry (two foundational properties of affective valuation) arise from a shared attentional mechanism. Consequently, these properties are contingent, dynamically coupled, and conditionally reducible, rather than fixed, independent, and irreducible axioms as assumed in classical behavioral economic theories. Furthermore, we map ARIA's computational components onto reward and interoceptive prediction errors, capturing how external and internal discrepancies jointly drive the construction of affective experience. Through numerical simulations and an initial empirical test, we show that ARIA reproduces classic affective phenomena, such as exponential decay, affective after-reactions, and alliesthesia, while also accounting for anomalous patterns, including cases in which environmental improvements fail to elicit pleasure and conditions under which inherently positive stimuli adapt more slowly than negative ones. Ultimately, ARIA offers a tractable computational framework for explaining affective dynamics and generating testable predictions about well-being and environmental experience.

articles_hidden.title: The Temporal Dynamics of Cognitive Control at Short and Long Timescales
articles_hidden.authors: Su Wang; Jacob Sellers; Han Zhang; Jahla Osborne; Taraz Lee; John Jonides
articles_hidden.abstract: Response-conflict tasks, such as the Simon and flanker tasks, are widely used to study how individuals exert cognitive control to override prepotent automatic responses (habits) in favor of goal-directed actions (goals). As task demands vary—from local, trial-by-trial interference to global changes in conflict frequency—control parameters may need to be adjusted to maintain task performance. Such cognitive control adaptations can be examined through congruency sequence effects (CSE, the congruency effect is reduced following an incongruent trial compared to a congruent trial) and list-wide proportional congruency effects (LWPCE, the congruency effect is reduced in mostly incongruent compared to mostly congruent blocks). Although both effects involve adjustments in control, it remains unclear whether these adjustments reflect similar or different mechanisms. Here, we used a “forced-response” paradigm combined with a computational model to understand the temporal dynamics of cognitive control that contribute to CSE and LWPCE. This approach allowed us to decompose cognitive control into the latencies of habitual and goal-directed processing and the probabilities with which these processes are expressed as overt behavior. We found that both recent conflict (driving the CSE) and frequent conflict within a block (driving the LWPCE) accelerated goal-directed processing and—in the Simon task only—increased the likelihood of inhibiting the habitual output; the LWPCE persisted after accounting for previous-trial congruency and thus could not be fully reduced to an accumulation of the CSE. These findings indicate that cognitive control adaptations share a common computational signature when regulating conflicts at both short and long timescales.

articles_hidden.title: Collective Effervescence as a Mediator between Emotion and Enjoyment in Live Dance
articles_hidden.authors: Ondine Simonot-Bérenger; Haeeun Lee; Matthias Sperling; Laura Rai; Julie Grezes; Guido Orgs
articles_hidden.abstract: Live performance provides a paradigmatic setting for collective aesthetic experiences, where the social dynamics shape how audiences perceive and evaluate performances. Building on prior research demonstrating that collective effervescence mediates the relationship between spectators' affective responses and enjoyment in live theatre, the present paper tests whether this same pathway generalises to two contemporary dance choreographies. In Study 1 (Detective Work, N=121), we examined both live (N=65) and screened (N=56) performances, distinguishing between connectedness to audience members and connectedness to performers. Unlike findings in live theatre, valence rather than arousal predicted enjoyment indirectly through connectedness, with performers-connectedness emerging as the stronger mediator in the screened modality, but not formally in the live one. Study 2 (Readings of what was never written, N=73) employed a reduced collective effervescence scale including both connectedness and sacredness facets; sacredness emerged as the dominant mediator of enjoyment, despite substantial covariance between facets. Across both studies, valence reliably predicted enjoyment through collective effervescence, whereas arousal effects were not detected; a sensitivity analysis indicates limited power to detect arousal effects in this sample, so this asymmetry is best read as a candidate dance-specific signature rather than a confirmed dissociation from narrative theatre. These findings extend theoretical models of aesthetic appreciation, indicating that while the core mediation pathway might generalise across performing arts, the most salient facet of collective effervescence and the dominant social tie can vary with artistic form, scale, and dramaturgical design.

articles_hidden.title: MDMA as a Means of Augmenting Exposure Therapy in the Context of Social Anxiety Disorder
articles_hidden.authors: Jason B Luoma; M. Kati Lear; Brian Pilecki
articles_hidden.abstract: Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD) presents a significant barrier to social and work functioning, and while exposure therapy has been a cornerstone of treatment, its effectiveness varies across individuals. This paper discusses how 3,4-Methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) may be used to enhance the effectiveness of an exposure-based intervention in SAD treatment. MDMA, known for its capacity to enhance feelings of social safeness, may enhance exposure therapy through a variety of mechanisms such as reducing safety behaviors, increasing contact with cues for core SAD fears, increasing expectancy violations, and increasing willingness. We explore the neurobiological and psychological underpinnings relevant to this augmentation strategy, particularly MDMA’s modulation of serotonin and dopamine pathways and its tendency to elicit self-transcendent positive emotions such as love, compassion, and gratitude. We also discuss recent findings suggesting that MDMA may open a window of neuroplasticity after administration during which effective exposure practice may have larger effects. To provide an illustration of these concepts, we describe how these ideas are being used to guide in vivo and imaginal exposure interventions as part of our clinical trial of MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder.  Ethical considerations, potential risks, and a framework for future empirical studies to test this theory are outlined. This approach could potentially offer a more profound and enduring therapeutic impact for those struggling with SAD, suggesting a promising area for further research.

articles_hidden.title: Shape is a good cue, not a ubiquitous one: lexical statistics of early nouns in English and Korean
articles_hidden.authors: Samah Abdelrahim; Jongmin Jung; Eon-Suk Ko; Michael C. Frank
articles_hidden.abstract: The shape bias, children's tendency to generalize new words by shape, is well documented in English-speaking children and reportedly weaker in children acquiring typologically different languages such as East Asian languages. One prominent explanation for the shape bias, the statistical generalization account, attributes the bias to the distributional dominance of shape-organized nouns in the early lexicon. We investigated this hypothesis, asking English and Korean adults to rate early-acquired common nouns. Most nouns were rated as solid and countable. In English speakers' ratings, far fewer were rated by shape than the account predicts, shape was chosen less often than material, and there were no detectable differences in the distribution of shape ratings across 16 languages' unilemma sets. Korean adults did not rate nouns as less shape-organized than English adults, contrary to what the weaker shape bias reported for East Asian language-speaking children would predict. Procedural differences had a large effect on the rate of shape organization. Despite these results, higher shape ratings were associated with earlier average age of acquisition, while solidity and countability, which are far more common, did not add unique predictive value in the pooled English-rated model. These findings suggest that shape may be a good cue for early noun learning, but not a ubiquitous or distinctively informative one relative to others, and that distributional differences may not be the key locus for cross-linguistic variation.

articles_hidden.title: Sleep, emotion regulation and mental well-being across culture: A pre-registered moderated mediation pathway
articles_hidden.authors: Narjis Fatima; Samantha Gregory; Robert Colin Alan Bendall
articles_hidden.abstract: Sleep quality and emotion regulation are associated with mental well-being. However, limited research has examined these relationships within a culturally informed framework, and importantly, it remains unknown whether emotion regulation strategies explain the relationship between sleep quality and well-being differently across cultural orientations. This study investigated whether cognitive reappraisal and expressive suppression mediated the relationship between sleep quality and mental well-being and whether these pathways varied according to cultural orientation. A pre-registered, cross-sectional online survey was completed by 598 adults residing in the United Kingdom or Pakistan. Participants completed measures of sleep quality, emotion regulation, mental well-being, and individualism–collectivism. Poor sleep quality predicted lower mental well-being and lower use of cognitive reappraisal. Cognitive reappraisal mediated the relationship between sleep quality and well-being, indicating that poorer sleep was associated with reduced use of cognitive reappraisal, which in turn predicted lower well-being. Cultural orientation moderated the relationship between expressive suppression and well-being, with expressive suppression becoming less adaptive at higher levels of individualism, but more positively associated with well-being at higher levels of collectivism. Participants from the United Kingdom reported greater use of cognitive reappraisal relative to expressive suppression, whereas participants from Pakistan demonstrated greater reliance on expressive suppression. Across both groups, greater dominance of cognitive reappraisal over expressive suppression predicted higher well-being. The findings indicate that sleep quality, emotion regulation, and cultural orientation are interconnected components of mental well-being and extends understanding of the cultural fit hypothesis, contributing to culturally informed models of emotion regulation and psychological well-being.

articles_hidden.title: Psychometric Validation of the English and Hindi Version of the Self-Compassion Scale for Youth (SCS-Y) among Indian Adolescents
articles_hidden.authors: Ekta Chopra; Yuki Miyagawa; Pushpita Behera; Pooja Sahni
articles_hidden.abstract: Research on self-compassion has consistently provided evidence for adolescent mental health. Within this, the Self-Compassion Scale for Youth (SCS-Y) is often used as a popular measure for assessing adolescent self-compassion. Although the psychometric properties of the scale establish it as a reliable and valid measure in Western samples, further studies need to examine any cultural and linguistic variations in this scale. The present study aims to fill this gap and investigates the factorial validation of the SCS-Y in Indian adolescents. This study provides evidence for the factor validation of both its original English version and an adapted Hindi version, extending the original findings for the U.S. sample. Across the two studies with large samples (ntotal=1,614; nstudy1=900, nstudy2=714), this study tested nine proposed models using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and exploratory structural equation modelling (ESEM). Findings revealed that the six-factor ESEM was found most favourable for the English SCS-Y version (Study 1; SCS-Y, English), while the two-bifactor CFA provided adequate fit for the Hindi SCS-Y version (Study 2; SCS-Y, Hindi). The results converged using model fit indices, factor loadings, and reliability analyses together for both English and Hindi versions. Uniquely, the adapted Hindi scale provided acceptable validity and reliability, confirming its suitable use for adolescents’ measurement of self-compassion. Overall, the study provided evidence for the use of six subscales for the SCS-Y, with additional two general scores of compassionate and uncompassionate self-responses for the Hindi version. Investigation of demographic variables revealed significantly higher self-judgement, isolation, and over-identification among girls and older adolescents, while grade-wise, those in higher grades were found to engage in significantly higher over-identification. Findings attest to the replicability of the SCS-Y among Indian adolescents while also providing current evidence of its factorial validity for both English and Hindi versions. Results from the study are implied in the context of adolescent mental health.

articles_hidden.title: Theoretical Challenges in Psychology in the 2000s: Top-5
articles_hidden.authors: Vladislav Medintsev
articles_hidden.abstract: Psychology entered the twenty-first century with an exceptionally large empirical base and a conspicuously thin theoretical infrastructure. The expansion of cognitive neuroscience, the institutionalization of evidence-based practice, and mounting evidence of a replication crisis exposed foundational assumptions to scrutiny of a kind the discipline had not faced since the paradigm debates of the mid-twentieth century. This article offers a structured critical overview of the five most consequential theoretical problems that shaped psychological science between 2000 and 2010 and traces their trajectory through 2026. The problems are ranked according to three explicit criteria—logical priority, breadth of disciplinary impact, and urgency for scientific and applied practice—and the ranking itself is defended as an argument, with alternative orderings considered and rejected. The resulting order is: (1) fragmentation of psychological theory and the absence of a unifying metatheory; (2) the crisis of construct validity and operationalism; (3) the mind–brain identity problem and the reductionism debate; (4) the cultural challenge to universalist assumptions; and (5) the methodological–epistemological tension between positivist and interpretivist traditions. Each problem is analyzed with respect to its antecedents, its specific manifestations during the 2000s, and the partial responses advanced in the subsequent decade and a half. The central claim is that the five problems form an interlocking system whose keystone is metatheoretical fragmentation; because the terms in which the remaining four problems are stated presuppose unsettled metatheoretical commitments, piecemeal reform cannot produce durable resolution. The concluding section outlines a research agenda centered on integrative theoretical reconstruction and epistemologically grounded methodological pluralism.

articles_hidden.title: People will buy non-cooperative rules
articles_hidden.authors: Connie Pui Yee Chiu; Ana Gantman
articles_hidden.abstract: Institutional rules enable large-scale human coordination, allowing strangers to cooperate by adhering to official rules that apply to all. Yet not all rules serve these cooperative ends. Why do they persist? Across three pre-registered experiments in the United States and China (N = 1610) players could buy rules in a Dictator Game. Even when the rules available for purchase did not serve cooperative ends, nearly half of U.S. participants (Study 1) and two-thirds of the Chinese participants (Study 2) bought at least one rule—more than the 33% that a separate sample of Americans forecasted would be willing to pay, and despite judging them to be of little utility. Both preferences for obedience (in the United States and China) and support for anti-democratic practices (United States) predicted “non-cooperative” rule purchasing, a phenomenon specific to non-cooperative rules as preferences for obedience predicted buying “non-cooperative” but not cooperative rules (Study 3).

articles_hidden.title: Does time dominate space? Testing Navon's (1978) conceptual hierarchy with public data
articles_hidden.authors: Adam Y. Shavit
articles_hidden.abstract: People often say where and when something happens in one sentence. Navon (1978) proposed a hierarchy behind such descriptions: time dominates space, and space dominates every other dimension. He gave three criteria for dominance (orderliness, change and scope), each a pattern that would show people treating one dimension as the frame for another, with examples but no data. We know of no direct test since. We apply two of his criteria, scope and change, and a processing test he cited, to public data in four studies without new participants. We recorded the predictions of each study and each registered extension before reading the data they would use. Analyses added later are labelled post hoc. Two AI coders of one model family worked independently on two English text collections annotated for grammar. They found a place stated at a time ("by six the children were home") about three times as often as a time stated at a place. After weighting the sample to match the whole corpus, the share was 0.74 of sentences in which one dimension restricts the other (95% interval 0.56 to 0.89). Two Indonesian collections of the same kind gave 0.70 (0.58 to 0.80; 70 such sentences among 6,628, fewer than the 100 its plan required). Of the 27 sampled dictionary definitions of change verbs, such as grow and fade, that say what the change happens over, 23 say time. Both language results favor Navon's hierarchy, but neither fully tells it apart from the alternative, left open by Garner (1976), that one dimension logically depends on the other. Navon cited the Garner interference criterion as evidence of a hierarchy in processing: if variation in one dimension slows judgments of a second dimension, but variation in the second does not slow judgments of the first, the first dominates. He added that his conceptual order need not match processing. Applying the interference criterion to 64 experiments from 39 papers, only the effect of space (extent or distance) on time reached significance in 25, and only that of time on space in 14 (both in 22, neither in 3). Of 32 sources on errors, disorders and related evidence such as gesture and language change, none shows time dominating space, and two partly support it. An appendix models the hierarchy with one score per dimension and gives sample sizes for future studies. Across the present studies, the language results have time dominating place, while the interference results lean toward space dominating time.

articles_hidden.title: EEG and self-report reveal preserved explicit appraisal of others’ pain but reduced modulation of affective and sensorimotor responses in autistic adults
articles_hidden.authors: Igor Riečanský; Ekaterina Pronizius; Martin Marko; Milan Mitka; Andreas de Lorenzo; Claus Lamm
articles_hidden.abstract: Empathy for pain—sharing another person’s affective state while maintaining self–other distinction—triggers sensorimotor and cognitive-emotional responses in the observer. We investigated whether these processes differ in autistic adults (ASD) and non-autistic controls (CON). Twenty ASD and 21 matched CON viewed images of a hand being either gently touched with a cotton bud or injected with a needle. For injection trials, participants were informed whether the target could feel pain (pain-sensitive) or not (pain-insensitive, due to local anesthesia), allowing assessment of how cognitive appraisal of the target’s pain sensitivity contributes to the empathic responses and their context-dependent modulation. EEG recorded sensorimotor engagement via event-related desynchronization (ERD) of central mu (7–13 Hz) and beta (14–25 Hz) rhythms. Participants also rated the target’s pain and their own unpleasantness. Both groups rated pain-sensitive injections as more painful than pain-insensitive injections, with no group differences, indicating comparable explicit appraisal of others’ pain in ASD and CON. In contrast, self-reported unpleasantness and ERD were modulated by target pain sensitivity only in CON, who reported greater unpleasantness and stronger mu ERD when the target could feel pain vs. not; this modulation was absent in ASD. No group differences emerged for touch or pain-insensitive injections, and viewing perspective (egocentric vs. altercentric) did not differentially affect responses. These findings suggest preserved explicit appraisal of others’ pain in autistic adults but reduced contextdependent modulation of affective and sensorimotor responses, pointing to a selective alteration in affective and sensorimotor sharing rather than a global empathy impairment in ASD.

articles_hidden.title: Moral Preferences Theory of Redistribution
articles_hidden.authors: Elijah Paul Galvan; Alan Sanfey
articles_hidden.abstract: In recent years, the steady rise of economic inequality across the globe has accompanied an ever-increasing focus on the question of redistribution. Though the majority of people believe that economic inequality is a problem, policy decisions to redistribute resources are typically highly contentious. Previous psychological, sociological, and political science theories which attempt to explain the paradox between stated beliefs and actual behavior in redistributive choice have largely relied upon an unverified assumption that redistributive preferences are derived from perceptions about pre-existing inequality. Here, we propose a Moral Preferences Theory of Redistribution, which integrates intuitions and prior research derived from various modeling frameworks across psychology, cognitive neuroscience, and economics.
