This theory posits that that redistributive behavior is guided by multiple moral principles, and that the preferences that guide the selection of these principles are both context-dependent and reflect dispositional individual values. This theory was tested using a multi-methodological approach: across two experiments – a large behavioral experiment (N = 231) and a direct fMRI follow-up study (N = 50) – the data show converging evidence to support the Moral Preferences Theory across multiple levels of analysis: political, psychometric, computational, and neural.

articles_hidden.title: “The Reports of My Death Are Greatly Exaggerated”: Humans Can Extract Unconscious Bigram Knowledge in the Artificial Grammar Learning Task
articles_hidden.authors: Andrei Preda; Andrei Razvan Costea; Adrian Opre; Răzvan Juchiș
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans often appear to possess knowledge they cannot fully articulate. For instance, in the landmark artificial grammar learning (AGL) task, participants acquire knowledge of a complex regularity (grammar) that structures letter sequences, while typically claiming to have little or no subjective access to the regularity, suggesting that learning has been largely unconscious. A highly influential argument against this conclusion comes from studies showing that participants can identify simple letter pairs (bigrams) that the grammar is composed of when asked to do so. Consequently, the unconscious status of learning in AGL has remained highly controversial. Crucially, however, these latter studies have never measured participants’ subjective states when performing the bigram identifications but have assumed that bigram identification necessarily reveals conscious knowledge. In this paper, we test this critical assumption by employing novel bigram-based artificial grammars and, simultaneously, by measuring participants’ subjective access to their bigram knowledge. For generalization, we employed both typical letter stimuli and face stimuli. Participants (N = 188) memorized strings (of faces or letters) constructed from the grammars; subsequently, they classified novel strings (half grammatical, half nongrammatical), reporting subjective awareness trial-by-trial. We found that letter strings were classified above chance based both on unconscious and on conscious knowledge (all ps < .001, Bayes factors > 10⁷), while data were insensitive for the faces condition (Bayes factors between 0.33 and 3). Our findings demonstrate unconscious learning of bigrams for letter strings, challenging the influential idea that accurate bigram knowledge necessarily reveals conscious knowledge.

articles_hidden.title: Pictorial Drug Cue Databases: A Systematic Review on the Publicly Available Resources and Their Methodological Parameter Space

articles_hidden.abstract:
Background
The cue-reactivity paradigm is widely used to study cue-induced responses across neural, cognitive, and behavioral domains in substance use disorder. Pictorial cues depicting drugs and related stimuli (e.g., syringes, lighters) are frequently used to elicit craving responses. However, substantial variability exists in the development, validation, and application of pictorial drug cue databases, limiting cross-study comparability.
 
Methods
This systematic review provides an overview of publicly available pictorial drug cue databases, summarizing key characteristics, validation processes, and assessment measures. A PubMed search (last run on February 9, 2026) was conducted for studies published through December 2025. Included studies developed publicly available pictorial cue databases, tested them in people with substance use, and evaluated affective (e.g., craving, valence, arousal) and/or cognitive (e.g., familiarity, typicality, complexity) measures.
 
Results
Of 1,692 records, 33 studies were included, introducing 36 distinct pictorial cue databases comprising 4,366 drug-related (74%) and 1,503 neutral (26%) images. Alcohol-related cues were the most common (67%), followed by nicotine (16%), cannabis (9%), methamphetamine (4%), and opioids (3%). Validation sample sizes ranged from 15 to 1,008 participants. Affective/motivational measures (e.g., craving, valence, arousal) were assessed in all 33 studies, but cognitive measures (e.g., familiarity, typicality, complexity) were included in only 9 (27%). Neural and physiological validation methods were used in 5 (15%) and 7 (21%) studies, respectively.
 
Conclusions
This review highlights considerable heterogeneity and gaps in cue database development and validation. We propose recommendations for developing, validating, and optimizing future databases to improve methodological rigor and replicability.

articles_hidden.title: AX-CPT Measures Show Good Reliability and Shared Variance, but Raise Concerns About Their Validity
articles_hidden.authors: Niels Oliver Kempkens; Alodie Rey-Mermet
articles_hidden.abstract: Attentional control refers to the ability to maintain a goal and goal-relevant information in the face of distraction. Previous research has highlighted the lack of reliability and shared variance in attentional-control measures. This may result from the heterogeneity of the control processes induced by the tasks. The aim of the present study was to reduce or control for this heterogeneity in two ways. First, we used one task – the AX-CPT – with different stimulus materials (letters, words, dot patterns, matrices, and pictures). In this task, a target response is required in trials where two specific stimuli occur in sequence (e.g., the letter “A” followed by the letter “X”). In all other trials, a non-target response is required. Second, we distinguished between proactive control (goal maintenance) and reactive control (goal reactivation) by computing separate indices for each process. Using data from 667 young adults, we obtained good reliability for most indices. Confirmatory factor analysis identified models with factors representing shared variance across stimulus materials. In a subsequent analysis, we bypassed the indices by modeling proactive and reactive control directly from error rates and response times. Using a bifactor modeling approach, we found shared variance across stimulus materials for error rates only. However, in both analyses, the pattern of latent correlations contradicted the expectations. For example, a positive and very high correlation was observed between indices representing proactive and reactive control. Overall, these findings raise concerns about the validity of AX-CPT measures.

Whether bilingualism is associated with network segregation across adulthood, and how these associations vary with language experience, remains unclear. To address this question, the present multisite study examines resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) among the Language network, the Default Mode (DMN), and the Multiple Demand (MD) (which support language processing, internally directed cognition, and domain-general cognitive control, respectively). Together, these findings highlight age-related reductions in network segregation and demonstrate that bilingual language experience is associated with systemic differences in large-scale functional network organization across adulthood.

Abstract

Objective: This protocol describes a reproducible mixed-methods workflow to derive symptom indicators from forum posts and examine their organisation relative to HiTOP. Two experts will qualitatively review the most frequent canonical symptom labels (at least 1,000) and develop a codebook of symptom categories, continuing until a prespecified saturation criterion is met. An LLM will assign canonical symptom labels to these categories, producing binary post-level indicators. Evaluation will assess interpretability, stability, and agreement with expert mapping to HiTOP. Supplementary analyses will include agent-assisted exploration, codebook application to DepressionEmo and the Reddit Mental Health Dataset, and pooled integrative analysis that may include additional comparable corpora.

Ethics: The Ethics Committee of Charité – Universitätsmedizin Berlin approved the study (EA2/274/25). The study was preregistered on 8 May 2026 (German Clinical Trials Register, DRKS00040244).

articles_hidden.title: Developmental Constraints on Learning and Liking Music
articles_hidden.authors: Nicholas Kathios; David Justin Vollweiler; Kelsie Lynn Lopez; Joel S. Snyder; Psyche Loui; Erin Hannon
articles_hidden.abstract:
Pleasure from sensory experience is thought to arise from the interplay between learned expectations and incoming stimuli, yet how this relationship develops across the lifespan is poorly understood. Lifetime exposure to culturally familiar stimuli confounds maturational differences in learning with differences in prior knowledge. We circumvent this problem by exposing children (5-12 years), adolescents (13-17 years), and young adults (19-24 years; total n = 237) to the Bohlen-Pierce scale, a musical system with no cultural tradition, and we manipulate exposure within a single session. All age groups formed expectations proportional to exposure, but only adolescents and adults were sensitive to structural violations in both familiarity judgments and aesthetic preference. While adults’ preference tracked exposure consistent with predictive coding accounts of reward, children preferences declined with repeated exposure.
The coupling between structural learning and hedonic experience increased across development, providing causal developmental evidence that pleasure from structured sensory input is constrained by the maturation of statistical learning.

articles_hidden.title: Artificial observers and real individual differences: A roadmap for a computational psychometrics of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly used as models of vision, yet they are evaluated against the average observer: average performance, average neural response, average representational geometry. This discards one of the richest constraints on theory: stable individual differences. Fitting the average is necessary but not sufficient. I argue that future models should be judged not only by their fit to mean human performance, but by whether populations of artificial observers reproduce the covariance structure and latent factors found across human observers. Two mature but disconnected literatures motivate this. Decades of factor-analytic psychophysics and electrophysiology show that interindividual variation is signal, not noise: the pattern of correlations among observers reveals the number and tuning of underlying mechanisms, and fractionates vision into many narrow factors rather than one general ability. Meanwhile, neural networks differing only in random initialization develop measurably different internal representations, so any single trained network is one sample from a distribution of possible observers. Joining these yields a computational psychometrics of vision: construct a designed population of artificial observers (varying in architecture, initialization, training diet, and front-end sampling), submit them to the same latent-variable analyses used on humans, and test whether the recovered factor structure matches. Recent work showing that seed-varied networks align with specific individuals is an existence proof. This article generalizes it into a framework, a staged roadmap, and a benchmark, together with the safeguards that keep such a benchmark from becoming an optimization target, for testing hypotheses about human visual variation with artificial observer populations.

articles_hidden.title: Not just looks, purposes, or essences: The role of causal structure in natural kind categorization
articles_hidden.authors: Ben Phillips; Eleonore Neufeld; Nestor Pinillos; Bob Rehder
articles_hidden.abstract: Several theories aim to explain how people categorize entities as members of natural kinds, but no study has systematically tested their competing predictions. We present four experiments that pit purely feature-based, psychological essentialist, teleological essentialist, causal-model, and dual-character accounts of natural-kind categorization against one another using a common set of vignettes. Across these experiments, we independently manipulated internal composition, appearance, telos, and the perceived causal relationships among them. We found that, while people tended not to treat any single feature as sufficient for category membership, internal composition was the strongest contributor to categorization judgments. In addition, categorization judgments depended on whether an entity’s composition stood in the appropriate causal relationships to its other features, rather than merely on whether those features were present. We also found little evidence for the dual-character view that natural-kind concepts involve distinct superficial and deeper criteria for category membership. Together, these findings favor a composition-centered causal-relational account of natural-kind categorization over its leading alternatives.

articles_hidden.title: Adaptivity complicates causality: How to evaluate the effects of adaptive support
articles_hidden.authors: Jasmin Breitwieser; Mirijam Schaaf; Garvin Brod
articles_hidden.abstract: Digital technologies make it possible to adapt the level of support to students’ behavior. However, determining what level is optimal for each student is methodologically challenging: If adaptations depend on prior behavior, adaptivity decisions are not fully randomized, which complicates causal inference. We present a methodological approach based on sequential experimental designs and directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to evaluate adaptivity decisions. We illustrate this approach in a mobile intervention promoting frequent vocabulary study. Students received planning prompts during a 20-day first-stage intervention, followed by an adapted prompting frequency in the second stage. Using a DAG, we formalized causal assumptions, identified confounding, and adjusted for it. The results illustrate the importance of this methodological approach to obtain valid causal conclusions: an unadjusted analysis would have led to the incorrect conclusion that scheduling more prompts leads to reduced study activity. This underscores the importance of making adaptivity decisions in an evidence-based way.

articles_hidden.title: Scientific inference with independent component analysis of functional MRI
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew Phillip Gunn; Morgan Pearlman; Chienyem Adaobi Nweke; Faithful Anane‑Asane; Sabadnoor Singh; Eden Tesfaye; Christine C. Minton
articles_hidden.abstract: Independent component analysis (ICA) provides spatial maps and time courses for studying task responses, functional connectivity, individual differences, and prediction. Their interpretation depends on the scientific question and how the measurements are constructed. We develop a conceptual framework linking the question, target quantity, ICA representation, analysis, and permissible conclusion. Its organizing argument is that representation estimation is part of measurement: model order, individual mapping, spatial constraints, and scaling influence what a network effect means. Using the same acquisition to study spatial organization or temporal coupling can require different estimators and validation evidence. We specify evidence that strengthens functional interpretation, separate BOLD physiology from decomposition assumptions, and distinguish association, reliability, longitudinal change, and causal effects. A hypothetical prediction study completes the reasoning by evaluating two locked models in independent participants, with uncertainty explicitly conditional on those fitted models. Worked reasoning examples and supplementary decision records make these choices inspectable, showing how the question determines the measurement, analysis, and evidence needed for a defensible answer.

articles_hidden.title: An Intuitive Physics Approach to Modeling Melodic Expectation
articles_hidden.authors: Breanna K. Nguyen; Jeremy Ng; Ilker Yildirim
articles_hidden.abstract: Humans have an intuitive understanding of music. We can predict the ensuing notes of a melody given the first few notes, but what computations drive these predictions? Other research theorizes about "musical forces"—forces analogous to how we represent the physical world—that might inform the way we form expectations about music. Here, we propose a new model of melodic expectation, the Probabilistic Musical Forces Model (PMFM), which formalizes melodic expectation as online probabilistic inference over latent melodic trajectories, inspired by force-based accounts of musical motion. The PMFM introduces a structured generative model that connects hidden melodic structure to observed sound by incorporating physical force-like relations. Like statistical models, the PMFM casts melodic expectation as probabilistic inference in a generative model, but unlike statistical models, the PMFM's generative model does not require learning from corpora. Instead, it is structured around a small set of force-like relational rules that operate over continuous latent states. Probabilistic inference in this generative model enables predicting the last note of a melody from its beginning notes. The PMFM strongly correlates with human performance in an existing dataset of melodic predictions. Compared with established statistical models, the PMFM, despite not being trained on corpora, explains similar or more variance in human data, including additional unique variance not explained by these models. Our model suggests that, beyond statistical learning, melodic expectation is also shaped by an "intuitive physics" basis.

articles_hidden.title: Sequential Priming Builder: A Free, No-Code Tool  for Implementing Sequential Priming Paradigms

articles_hidden.abstract: Sequential priming tasks are a family of methods widely used in psychology. articles_hidden.title: The Morality of Partiality: How Relationship Expectations Shape Moral Evaluations
articles_hidden.authors: Zuleykha Gasimova; Amiya Shelly Aggarwal; Jonathan Albert Fugelsang; Alexander C. Walker
articles_hidden.abstract: While impartiality is often regarded as a moral virtue, acting impartially can violate social expectations and relational obligations, creating tension between competing moral considerations. Across sacrificial dilemmas and more ecologically valid helping scenarios, partial actors were judged more moral and trustworthy than impartial actors. articles_hidden.title: Body image in relation to ADHD and ADHD traits: A mixed-methods scoping review
articles_hidden.authors: Phaedra Longhurst; Lauren Makin; Fidan Turk; Helena Lewis-Smith
articles_hidden.abstract:
Accumulating evidence suggests associations between ADHD, negative body image, and 
disordered eating; however, relatively little is known about how body image has been 
conceptualised, assessed, and experienced. This mixed-methods scoping review aimed to 
map and synthesise existing research examining body image in relation to ADHD and ADHD 
traits. Seven databases (Embase, CENTRAL, CINAHL, MEDLINE, PubMed, PsycINFO, and 
Scopus) and two grey literature sources (PsyArXiv and ProQuest) were searched from 
inception to September 2026. Data were charted iteratively and synthesised descriptively 
and narratively. Twenty-seven studies (25 quantitative, two qualitative) published between 
1995 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. All studies were based in Westernised contexts, 
with most employing cross-sectional designs. ADHD was predominantly assessed using
symptom-based measures and/or diagnostic status, while body image was most commonly 
assessed using subscales of the Eating Disorder Inventory. Quantitative studies primarily 
examined associations between ADHD and negative body image, with some evidence of 
greater negative body image in ADHD. However, findings were inconsistent across studies, 
particularly following adjustment for covariates (e.g., co-occurring psychopathology). The 
literature predominantly adopted pathology-oriented conceptualisations of body image, with 
no studies examining positive body image and limited exploration of lived 
experiences. Further gaps were identified in methodological approaches, the 
conceptualisation and measurement of body image and ADHD, and the representation of 
diverse populations. Reliance on predominantly neurotypical-derived conceptualisations and 
measurement tools not validated among ADHD samples raises concerns about their 
validity. Future research should prioritise participatory approaches to advance an inclusive, 
neuro-affirming understanding of body image among the ADHD population.

articles_hidden.title: Psychological dimensions of wise reasoning
articles_hidden.authors: Veronica Diveica; Bri Susanna Darboh; Roni Setton; Gary R. Turner; R. Nathan Spreng
articles_hidden.abstract: Wise reasoning is an adaptive capacity associated with wellbeing and pro-sociality across the lifespan, yet why some individuals reason more wisely than others remains unclear. Although most associations were similar across age groups, some evidence of age-related moderation emerged, including stronger associations with autobiographical memory vividness among younger adults and openness to experience among older adults. The correlates of wise reasoning did not fully generalize to self-reported wisdom traits, which were associated primarily with self-reported personality and affective dispositions. These findings advance an integrated account of the psychological foundations of wise reasoning across adulthood, highlighting their multidimensional nature, relative stability across the adult lifespan, and the key roles of autobiographical memory and crystallized cognition.

articles_hidden.title: Emotion dysregulation in everyday life among children with ADHD: A cross-cultural qualitative study of parents’ accounts in Belgium and China
articles_hidden.authors: Canmei Xu; Lisa B Thorell; Mariette Huizinga; Ruwen Liang; Dieter Baeyens
articles_hidden.abstract: Emotional dysregulation (ED) is frequently observed among children with ADHD, yet little is known about how it unfolds in everyday life, particularly across cultural contexts. This qualitative study examined ED in primary school-aged children with ADHD in a Western cultural context (Belgium) and an Eastern cultural context (China). articles_hidden.title: Individual and environmental predictors of math anxiety in primary school children
articles_hidden.authors: Monika Szczygieł; Mateusz Hohol
articles_hidden.abstract: Previous meta-analyses have indicated that math anxiety (MA) is weakly to moderately and negatively related to math achievement, yet relatively few studies have simultaneously examined a range of predictors of MA and the proportion of variance in MA explained by these predictors. articles_hidden.title: The cortical representation of materials and their properties
articles_hidden.authors: Hua-Chun Sun; Martin N Hebart; Filipp Schmidt; Roland Fleming

articles_hidden.title: Recovery Capital, Structural Barriers, and Wellbeing Among Adults in Addiction Recovery: Findings from the Life in Recovery Survey in Spain

articles_hidden.title: Reward sensitivity is associated with gambling participation, and financial vulnerability with problem gambling in U.S. adults
articles_hidden.authors: Cooper Joseph Sharp; Arunachalam Lakshmanan; Mariami Sakhiashvili; Elizabeth Newnam; Jeremy Mennis; David Victor Smith
articles_hidden.abstract: The rapid expansion of legal and online gambling in the United States has renewed public-health concern about gambling participation and gambling-related problems. articles_hidden.title: Private Practitioners’ Use and Perceptions of Digital Mental Health Tools to Support Evidence-based Youth Psychotherapy

Background: Mental health clinicians in private practice represent approximately half of the outpatient workforce. Clinicians in this environment have more global negative attitudes toward implementing evidence-based treatments (EBTs), despite the proven efficacy of EBTs in treating children and adolescents. Digital mental health (DMH) tools may help streamline EBT implementation, thus reducing demands on clinicians. However, little is known about how clinicians in this group perceive and use DMH tools with youth. 

Objective: This mixed methods study examined how clinicians in private practice currently use and perceive DMH tools. 

Method: Explanatory sequential design included survey data collection from 79 master’s- and doctoral-level licensed clinicians in two large, diverse urban regions within the U.S. Qualitative interviews were completed subsequently with 15 clinicians for purposes of thematic analysis.

Conclusions: DMH tools are being used to support elements of EBTs, and could reduce time spent out of session on tracking, preparation, and documentation for private practice clinicians. Future research should address barriers identified here in user-centered design processes with this group.

articles_hidden.title: Questionable mediated effect of Tai Chi exercise on psychological distress in older adults: A reassessment of Xu and Yang (2026)
articles_hidden.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen
articles_hidden.abstract: Xu and Yang concluded an association between Tai Chi exercise and reduced psychological distress among older adults, and that this association was mediated by reduced negative mood state and increased sleep quality. However, mediated effects, like correlations in general, in observational data may be spurious, e.g., due to confounding by a shared cause of the variables. Here, a reassessment indicated that direct, indirect (i.e., mediated), and total effects of Tai Chi exercise on psychological distress reported by Xu and Yang were indistinguishable from effects implied by a model where the measured variables were specified as indicators of a shared latent cause. Hence, the effects reported by Xu and Yang may have been spurious and their conclusions premature. Researchers are recommended to evaluate if mediated effects survive adjustment for a potential shared cause of the predictor, mediator(s), and outcome before making claims about genuine mediation.
